en: The Mañjuśrī-mūla-kalpa, a Text of the Great Vaipulya Bodhisattva-piṭaka, Fascicle One.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heavens, Chao-san Dafu, Acting Assistant Director of the Court of State Ceremonial.
Translated by the Great Master Mingjiao, Subject Tianxi-zai, by Imperial Decree. Chapter One: The Introduction. Thus have I heard.
At one time, the World-Honored One...
In the celestial realm of Pure Light, there was an unprecedented assembly of inconceivable and pure bodhisattvas at the site of enlightenment.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Devaputra Pure Light.
Now, this Bodhisattva possesses the unprecedented, inconceivable conduct, supreme supernatural powers, transformations, samādhis, and the path of liberation of a bodhisattva;
by means of mantra syllables, he benefits all sentient beings, granting them freedom from illness and long life.
"May all sentient beings be perfected in wealth and nobility.
At that time, the devaputra Pure Light joined his palms in reverence and spoke these words.
This is the supreme samādhi practiced by bodhisattvas as taught by the World-Honored One:
sitting upon the vajra-seat, subduing demonic adversaries, turning the wondrous wheel of Dharma,
and practicing the conduct that is free from all the poverty, illness, and afflictions of the world.
The worldly mantras cause all aspirations to be fulfilled and bring about the benefit of all sentient beings in accordance with all the teachings of the Tathāgata.
"I have now reflected upon this matter in this way.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha, observing the Heaven of Pure Light,
entered a samādhi called "Pure Realm, Radiance that Dispels Darkness."
When he entered that samādhi,
a great radiance named "Illumination of Blooming Flowers" issued from between the eyebrows of the World-Honored One.
The Bodhisattva further emitted countless hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of light rays, which circled the Buddha three times;
having done so, they proceeded to the trichiliocosm.
Furthermore, passing beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of a hundred thousand Ganges Rivers to the northeast,
there is a world named Kāśapusa. Therein dwells the Buddha,
the World-Honored One, named Kāśapusarāja Tathāgata.
There was a youth there named Mañjuśrī.
Having practiced the power of great vows in the past,
he dwelt together with bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Having seen that light, he wore a smile upon his face and addressed the assembly of bodhisattvas, saying:
"Sons of the Buddha, this light illuminates us; let us go together."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta remained gazing with a joyful countenance toward the direction from which the light emanated. Then,
that light again illuminated that world, Padmavati, as well as its Blessed One, the Tathāgata Padmottara.
It circled three times more,
and then entered the crown of the head of the youth Mañjuśrī.
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī rose from his seat.
He circumambulated the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata King of Blossoming Flowers, three times;
he prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, knelt with his right knee on the ground,
and addressed the Tathāgata King of Blossoming Flowers, saying:
The World-Honored One, Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha,
has emitted light to summon me.
I now wish to go to the Sahā world to the presence of Śākyamuni Buddha.
I pay respectful homage.
I rejoice in all the secret ritual manuals for the accomplishment of mantra practices, the consecration of painted banners,
and the secret heart-seals (*hṛdaya-mudrā*) of the empowerment of all Tathāgatas.
"It can cause all the aspirations of all sentient beings to be fulfilled.
Having spoken thus,
at that time the Tathāgata King of Blossoming Flowers addressed the youth Mañjuśrī, saying:
Regarding all the aspirations and desires you now possess,
you should go there quickly;
if you see that Buddha Śākyamuni, [your wishes will be fulfilled].
Please convey my greetings and inquire after his well-being:
whether he has little illness and little affliction, and whether his daily life is light, easy, and lived in peace and happiness.
At that time, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Padmarāja, again addressed the youth Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Youth, these hundred thousand Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges..."
Through the secret ritual procedures for constructing the maṇḍala for mantra practice, the empowerment, the heart-seals (mudrā), the consecration of images, and the performance of homa,
all one’s aspirations shall be completely fulfilled.
This is the ritual for the "Precious Jewel Adored and Honored by All Sentient Beings," the mantra of the Wisdom King’s Sovereign Prophecy for the past, future, and present.
If one maintains and recites it, the land will be peaceful and happy, and one will be able to subdue all enemies.
This chapter on the ritual procedures explains how all mundane and supramundane Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and those on the Bodhisattva stages may receive,
practice, and teach it; having already taught this, he teaches it again.
I likewise rejoice with aspiration and delight.
O Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, regarding all that has transpired here, follow wherever you go;
before Śākyamuni Buddha, you shall hear this True Dharma.
Furthermore, I shall explain this mantra for you:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ mañjuśrīparatikṣiptaśāsanānām | Oṃ rara samara apratikṣiptaśāsana kumāra-rūpa-dharīṇa hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā*. This is the root mantra of the youth Mañjuśrī.
This is the heart-mantra of all Tathāgatas, proclaimed by all Tathāgatas in common;
I too shall speak it, and you now must speak it.
Go to the Sahā world-system.
He extensively explained how this can perform all the buddha-activities.
He further spoke the inner-heart mantra taught by Śākyamuni Tathāgata:
Oṃ vajranātha namas. He then spoke the outer-heart mantra.
Vajra hūṃ. At that time, the Tathāgata Padmavikrāmin taught a samādhi to the youth Mañjuśrī.
It is named "Adorning All Bodhisattva Practices to Attain Bodhi.
At that time, when the youth Mañjuśrī entered this samādhi,
the four directions became boundless and the zenith and nadir became vast and expansive.
All the Buddhas fill this world and further praise him, saying: "Excellent, excellent!
Son of the Buddha, you are able to enter this supreme samādhi."
All śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are unable to enter it;
even bodhisattva practitioners who have attained the ten stages (bhūmi) cannot enter this samādhi.
At that time, the Tathāgata King of Blooming Flowers—
that World-Honored One— likewise spoke this mantra for the accomplishment of all secret matters within the mind of the youth Mañjuśrī.
This is called the secret within a single syllable.
It causes all sentient beings to accomplish the supreme task;
even through other mantra practices, one attains the accomplishment of the supreme task.
At that time, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Padmarāja, remained silent for a moment.
With his Buddha-eye, he surveyed all worlds and all Buddhas.
Those World-Honored Ones, with compassionate intent, summoned him and requested that they together proclaim the mantra.
*Namo samantabuddhānām āḥ*. This is the inner heart-mantra of Mañjuśrī;
it is capable of accomplishing all activities.
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī arose from that samādhi.
In the time it takes for a strong man to bend and extend his arm,
he further attains the samādhi of swift wisdom,
named "Supreme Transformation."
By means of his supernormal powers, he traveled to the Sahā world in a single instant;
there, in the sky above the Heaven of Pure Light,
he sat upon a ground of great maṇi jewels.
He emitted a great radiance that illuminated all the devas of Pure Light.
This is the samādhi named "Illumination Adorned with Luminous Jewels.
When the youth Mañjuśrī entered this meditative absorption, [he performed these deeds].
There appeared countless pavilions adorned with jewels and countless jeweled canopies,
extending for hundreds of thousands of yojanas in length and breadth,
along with celestial robes, great garments, and various precious necklaces.
Pure and majestic celestial flowers, banners, and streamers were arrayed;
jeweled nets and bells emitted subtle and wondrous sounds;
furthermore, celestial powdered incense and scented powders rained down.
And when the bodhisattvas of the stage of non-retrogression made offerings to our World-Honored One,
Śākyamuni, at that time the devaputra Pure Light (Vimalaprabha) beheld those bodhisattvas’ supernatural transformations.
It was a most marvelous and unprecedented occurrence;
the hairs on his body all stood on end, and he trembled within the celestial palace, becoming dazed and struck with terror:
"How is it that my supernormal powers have now been utterly exhausted?"
Contemplating this sign, he cried out in a loud voice,
"O my Buddha Śākyamuni, may you deign to grant protection!
At that time, the World-Honored One Śākyamuni...
He addressed the devaputras of Pure Radiance, saying:
"Do not give rise to fear or alarm.
That noble one is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrīkumārabhūta."
From the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Flower-King,
he has come to my presence to pay respectful homage and to rejoice in this great matter:
the mantras, extensive discourses, and unprecedented, profound verses of the Dharma.
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī circumambulated the World-Honored One Śākyamuni three times,
prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, and gazed up at him with a joyful countenance.
With a subtle and wondrous voice, he spoke these words of praise:
"Homage to the Great Being, the Tamer; Homage to the Unsurpassed Great Being;
Homage to the Supreme Great Being, Who is able to bring all undertakings to fulfillment."
I take refuge in the Great Being who is like a lion, Who can destroy all evil deeds;
I take refuge in the Great Being who is fearless, Who can destroy all evil realms;
I take refuge in the Great Being who is like a white lotus, Whose fragrance of merit and wisdom is boundless.
I take refuge in the Great Being of the Lotus, Pure and transcending the mud of the triple world;
I take refuge in the Great Being of Liberation, Able to leave behind all suffering and affliction;
I take refuge in the Great Being of Quiescence, Able to skillfully subdue all that is evil.
I take refuge in the accomplished Great Being, who perfectly knows all true speech;
I take refuge in the auspicious Great Being, who can transform all inauspiciousness into auspiciousness;
I take refuge in the Buddha, the Great Being, who perfectly knows the treasury of all dharmas.
I take refuge in the Tathāgata, who has entered all phenomena, Truly into the non-conceptual reality;
I take refuge in the Tathāgata, the All-Knowing One, Whose wisdom of omniscience is free from illusory phenomena.
By means of the untainted paths of the three vehicles, He causes beings to enter and abide in nirvāṇa.
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī,
having offered praise and taken refuge, spoke again, saying:
"World-Honored One, I have traveled past worlds as numerous as the sands of hundreds of thousands of Ganges Rivers to the northeast."
In that realm there is a buddha-field named Kausumita.
Therein dwells a World-Honored One named Kausumitarāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
He teaches the Dharma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end;
its meaning is profound and its phrasing is exquisite;
it is pure, unadulterated, complete, and the very embodiment of the stainless holy life.
Thus he dwells securely in the characteristics of preaching the Dharma;
furthermore, he explains the meaning of the practice of mantras and cultivates the skillful means of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka for the sake of delivering sentient beings.
Causing them to practice the path of the three vehicles and attain profound peace and happiness,
he thus proclaims this for the sake of all those sentient beings.
When I came here, the Tathāgata Flower-King King of Flowers commanded me to pay homage at your feet and inquire after your well-being:
whether you have little illness and little affliction, and whether your daily life is light, easy, and lived in peace and happiness.
Śākyamuni Buddha is most rare and extraordinary;
appearing in the world during the final age to teach the Dharma,
he brings benefit, peace, and joy to humans and devas through the path of the Three Vehicles.
And all practice great diligence with equanimity to sever the suffering of the three realms,
causing those sentient beings to attain great peace and happiness on the path to nirvāṇa.
Thus does our Buddha, the World-Honored One, know this Buddha-mind.
The youth spoke again: "How can one attain the inconceivable and unprecedented?
How does the Buddha, the World-Honored One, through his sovereign transformations, mental wisdom, and mental activities, penetrate deeply into the characteristics of phenomena?"
For hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of eons,
they have expounded all those true dharmas, thoroughly destroying all marks of form,
and have ultimately realized the reality that transcends all signs.
"Such conduct and virtues of the World-Honored One can be known by him, but I cannot know them.
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī,
by means of his own supernatural power, manifested a great precious lotus throne.
Gazing up at the World-Honored One Śākyamuni,
at that time the World-Honored One Śākyamuni heard of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta.
With various modes of speech, he revealed the past deeds of the Tathāgata Flower King;
with the melodic resonance of a kalaviṅka bird, he expounded the profound and wondrous ritual procedures for the bodhisattva practices as he had vowed to do.
Skillfully responding to the various capacities of sentient beings, he addressed the youth Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Welcome, Mañjuśrī!
That superior person practices the Dharma taught by all Buddhas."
For the sake of all bodhisattvas,
may they obtain all mantra phrases, secret empowerments, mudrās, maṇḍalas, and ritual procedures;
may they enjoy long life, few illnesses, and sovereign mastery according to their wishes.
All is complete.
One attains the ritual procedures for the wisdom of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*).
This has been briefly explained regarding the past, future, and present.
May the aspirations of all sentient beings be fulfilled.
If one possesses the virtue of ethical discipline and transmits the mantra practices, others will come to love and respect them.
Whether seeking wisdom or wishing to become invisible, [may these goals be attained].
If one walks through space, one’s feet do not touch the ground;
or again, one may enter the earth or subdue all that is desired and attain it,
including yakṣas, yakṣīs, and the retinues of yakṣas.
All the Viśanis, Viśacis, and Bhūtas are completely subdued.
Whether young, in the prime of life, or aged, all shall attain long life.
In brief, all their wishes and desires will be fulfilled.
Regarding the rites of subjugation, augmentation,
and pacification, whatever is performed shall all be accomplished.
This is the Dharma Chapter on the Great Jewel Ritual Manual from the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, spoken by all Buddhas.
I cause you to know this treasury of the ritual procedures for the practice of mantras,
which can purify persons and benefit many people,
so that all sentient beings in the heavens and among humans may obtain peace and happiness.
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī entered the bodhisattva samādhi called "The Radiant Adornment of the Precious Jewels of the Majestic Power of All Buddhas.
Upon entering this concentration, he emitted a great radiance.
It illuminated Buddha-fields as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River,
as well as countless pure bodhisattvas,
extending upward as far as the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.
Reaching down as far as the Avīci Hell,
it causes all sentient beings suffering from the retribution of their sins to have their calamities and afflictions extinguished.
Having illuminated all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas, it...
It then re-entered the crown of the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī and further illuminated all the Buddha-fields and Tathāgatas throughout the eastern world-systems for the sake of the Dharma assembly.
Their names were:
the Tathāgata Śubhagandharvadyutiśrī, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyarāja-prabhā-rāja,
and the Tathāgata Samantāvabhāsa-śrī.
The Tathāgata Jātarāja,
the Tathāgata Śālarāja,
and the Tathāgata Maitreya.
Amitāyus Tathāgata; Samyaksaṃbuddhajñānarāja Tathāgata;
Anantaprabhārāja Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata King of Supreme Radiance,
and other such Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas,
each surrounded by a retinue of bodhisattvas.
They all gathered together in the Heaven of Pure Light (*Vimalaprabhā*).
At that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śākyamuni,
wishing for the sake of the youth Mañjuśrī—
This is the chapter on the ritual procedures for the meaning of the mantra phrases of the Bodhisattva practices.
At that time, there were also all the Buddhas from all the Buddha-fields in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, above, and below.
Their light shone everywhere as they also gathered for the assembly.
Each of those Buddhas was surrounded by a retinue of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas,
each desiring to follow their respective Buddha to hear and receive the Tathāgata’s unsurpassable teaching on the mantra rituals and the supreme samādhi.
Namely, the Bodhisattva Subāhu, the Bodhisattva Susārtha,
the Bodhisattva Sucīrṇa, the Bodhisattva Sunetra,
the Bodhisattva Sukhāvatī, and the Bodhisattva Sudharma.
The Bodhisattva Sarvārthasiddha, the Bodhisattva Sarvajanman,
the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, the Bodhisattva Ratnasaṃbhava,
the Bodhisattva Ratnaśrī, and the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī.
The Bodhisattva Acintyaśrī, the Bodhisattva Prabhāśrī,
the Bodhisattva Jyotiḥśrī, the Bodhisattva Jñānaśrī,
the Bodhisattva Sarvārthaśrī, and the Bodhisattva Sarvaratnapāṇi.
The Bodhisattva Ratnaśikhin, the Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi,
the Bodhisattva Citradhvajapāṇi, the Bodhisattva Samantāvabhāsagarbha,
the Bodhisattva Ratnagarbha, and the Bodhisattva Jñānagarbha.
The Bodhisattva Sublime Treasury of Thought, the Bodhisattva Dharma-Treasury,
the Bodhisattva Banner, the Bodhisattva Sublime Banner,
the Bodhisattva Boundless Banner, and the Bodhisattva Radiant Banner.
The Bodhisattva Vimaladhvaja, the Bodhisattva Anantadhvaja,
the Bodhisattva Gaganadhvaja,
and the Bodhisattva Ratnadhvaja.
The Bodhisattva Roaring Sound, the Bodhisattva King of Drum-Sound,
the Bodhisattva King of Boundless Illuminating Wisdom, the Bodhisattva King Who Shatters All Darkness,
the Bodhisattva King Who Shatters All Radiance, and the Bodhisattva King of Profound Wisdom in All Practices.
Bodhisattva Benevolent King, Bodhisattva Profound Meaning King,
Bodhisattva Elimination King, Bodhisattva Topknotless King,
Bodhisattva Sun King, and Bodhisattva Birth from Non-nature King.
The Bodhisattva King Born of Self-Nature and the Bodhisattva King Born of the Self-Nature of Non-Nature;
the Bodhisattva King of the Non-Retrogressive Stage, the Bodhisattva Sovereign Light,
the Bodhisattva Virtue Light, and the Bodhisattva World Light.
The Bodhisattva Amṛtaprabha, the Bodhisattva Anantaprabha,
the Bodhisattva Devendraprabha, the Bodhisattva Svabhāvaprabha,
the Bodhisattva Abhāvaprabha, and the Bodhisattva Antardhāna.
The Bodhisattva Asparśa,
the Bodhisattva Anabhisaṃskāra, the Bodhisattva Apariniṣṭhita, the Bodhisattva Vimala,
the Bodhisattva Anagni, and the Bodhisattva Sūti.
Bodhisattva Maitri, Bodhisattva Āgati,
Bodhisattva Sukha, Bodhisattva Mukha,
Bodhisattva Rimiṇimi, and Bodhisattva Ketu.
The Bodhisattva Ānanda,
the Bodhisattva Prabhāsa, the Bodhisattva Nīvara, the Bodhisattva Devātideva,
the Bodhisattva Nābhi, and the Bodhisattva Mahāratha.
The Bodhisattva Lokadhātu, the Bodhisattva Śāntikara,
the Bodhisattva Prāmodya, the Bodhisattva Dundubhisvara,
the Bodhisattva Siddhi, and the Bodhisattva Sitaprabha.
The Bodhisattva Pure Heaven of the Supreme Bodhisattvas;
the Bodhisattva Capable of Forbearance; the Bodhisattva Capable of Subduing;
the Bodhisattva Difficult to Attain; and the Bodhisattva of the Far-Reaching Journey.
The Bodhisattva Far-Removed, the Bodhisattva Dwelling Afar,
the Bodhisattva High, the Bodhisattva Utterly High,
the Bodhisattva Luminous as Space, and the Bodhisattva Universally Illuminating.
The Bodhisattva Svayamprabha, the Bodhisattva Rṣipravara,
the Bodhisattva Prabhāśuddha, the Bodhisattva Anabhirata,
the Bodhisattva Sumati, and the Bodhisattva Mahādeva.
The Bodhisattva Viśuddha, the Bodhisattva Vimala,
the Bodhisattva Dānta,
and the Bodhisattva Svapraśānta.
The Bodhisattva Subhavyūha, the Bodhisattva Śvetaketu,
the Bodhisattva Emeya,
and the Bodhisattva Kemeya.
The Bodhisattva Youth, the Bodhisattva Coolness,
the Bodhisattva Extended Life, the Bodhisattva Wondrous Birth,
the Bodhisattva Dark Banner, and the Bodhisattva Banner.
The Bodhisattva White Banner, the Bodhisattva Wondrous Banner, the Celestial Banner,
the Bodhisattva Abiding in Peace, the Bodhisattva Great Ancestor,
the Bodhisattva Father and Teacher, and the Bodhisattva Skillfully Understanding.
Bao-ping Bodhisattva, Shi-xian Bodhisattva,
Pu-xian Bodhisattva, Da-xian Bodhisattva,
Zeng-yi Bodhisattva, and Shen-guang Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva Kinkiara, the Bodhisattva Samacitta,
the Bodhisattva Lokahita, the Bodhisattva Sūryaprabha,
the Bodhisattva Dīpaṃkara, and the Bodhisattva Bahuśruta.
The Bodhisattva Sarvārthasiddha attained the accomplishment of a bodhisattva,
as did the Bodhisattvas Prabhākara, Avabhāsakara, Dundubhisvara, and Manojñasvara.
Bodhisattva Wondrous Sound,
Bodhisattva Boundless Sound,
and Bodhisattva Banner Sound.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Real-Ṛṣi (Sārṣi),
and other such Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas, gathered for this assembly.
Furthermore, there were the Tathāgatas of the seven Buddhas and the Tathāgata Golden-Ṛṣi (Suvarṇa-Ṛṣi).
The Tathāgata Kakuda, the Tathāgata Prabhāsa, the Tathāgata Agniskandha,
the Tathāgata Nirmāṇakārin, the Tathāgata Abhyudgata-darśana,
and the Tathāgata Śākyamuni— all such Buddhas were universally illumined by this light.
They came to the Śuddhāvāsakāyika Heaven and sat upon jewel lotuses.
There were also bodhisattva-mahāsattvas,
endowed with the marks of true physical form, who all came to the assembly and sat together.
They are as follows:
the Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the Bodhisattva Supāṇi,
the Bodhisattva Gaganapāṇi, and the Bodhisattva Anantapāṇi.
The Bodhisattva Earth-Hand, the Bodhisattva World-Hand,
the Bodhisattva Profoundly Pure, the Bodhisattva Wondrous Accumulation,
the Bodhisattva Great Accumulation, and the Bodhisattva Maṇi-Jewel Accumulation.
Bodhisattva Ratnagaja, Bodhisattva Samantagaja,
Bodhisattva Gandhahastin, Bodhisattva Sucarita,
Bodhisattva Viśuddhacārin, and Bodhisattva Lokacārin.
The Bodhisattva Swift Traveler, the Bodhisattva Boundless Practice,
the Bodhisattva Boundless Renown, the Bodhisattva Wondrous Renown,
the Bodhisattva Stainless Renown, and the Bodhisattva Practice Renown.
The Bodhisattva Vimalakīrti is called the Bodhisattva,
the Honored Bodhisattva, the Bodhisattva who is Honored by the Unhonored,
the World-Honored Bodhisattva, and the Universally Honored Bodhisattva.
Maitreya Bodhisattva, Anantamaitrī Bodhisattva,
Samatāmaitrī Bodhisattva, Maitreya Bodhisattva,
Sunetramaitrī Bodhisattva, and Amitamaitrī Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva Compassion of the Three Times is the True Bodhisattva;
the Bodhisattva Compassion of the Triple Gem is the Bodhisattva of the Three Refuges;
the Bodhisattva Compassion of the Three Vehicles is the Transformation Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva Subhāṣitamati, the Bodhisattva Dharmavaśavartin,
the Bodhisattva Abhāvavaśavartin, the Bodhisattva Samantavaśavartin,
the Bodhisattva Lokavaśavartin, and the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, the Bodhisattva Paramāvalokiteśvara;
the Honored One among Worldly Bodhisattvas, the Most Sublime Honored One among Bodhisattvas;
the Bodhisattva Dundubhisvara-nirghoṣa, the Bodhisattva Viśuddheśvara.
The Bodhisattva Citta-vaśitā (Mastery of Mind), the Bodhisattva Ārya-gaṇa (Holy Multitude),
the Bodhisattva Su-lakṣaṇa (Excellent Marks), the Bodhisattva Jina-vara (Supreme Victor),
the Bodhisattva Yaśas-kīrti (Renowned Name), and the Bodhisattva Sūrya-prabha (Sunlight).
The Bodhisattva Prabhāsvara, the Bodhisattva Suśaśvata,
the Bodhisattva Śubha, the Bodhisattva Suśubha,
the Bodhisattva Anantakīrti, and the Bodhisattva Samantakīrti.
The Bodhisattva Lokamaṅgala, the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja,
the Bodhisattva Gaganaiśvaragarbha, the Bodhisattva Bhūmīśvara,
the Bodhisattva Maheśvara, and the Bodhisattva Mahābhūmi.
Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva, Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin Bodhisattva,
Samantavijaya Samantabhadra Bodhisatva, Bhadrapāla Bodhisattva,
Ratnacandra Bodhisattva, and Praśāntacitta Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva Sublime Flower, the Bodhisattva Sublime Space,
the Bodhisattva Space Treasury, the Bodhisattva Treasury of All Meanings,
and the Bodhisattva Source of All.

This is a brief explanation of the ritual manual for the principles of the meaning of mantra practice.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is endowed with one single dharma, they will attain accomplishment in mantra practice.
What is this one dharma?
If one can contemplate and perceive the unimpeded characteristic of the single dharma of dharmas,
one will attain the accomplishment of the mantra.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in two dharmas,
they will further achieve success in the practice of mantra.
What are these two dharmas?
Without departing from the bodhicitta,
one maintains an equanimous mind toward all sentient beings;
through these two dharmas, one accomplishes the mantra.
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in three dharmas,
they will achieve accomplishment in the fundamental practice of mantras.
What are these three dharmas?
One does not abandon or forsake the minds of all sentient beings;
one diligently guards and upholds the bodhisattva precepts and practices;
and one firmly maintains and never forgets the fundamental conduct of mantras.
Thus, these three dharmas accomplish the mantra.

One attains accomplishment in the practice of mantra.
What are the four dharmas?
They are as follows: namely, not abandoning the original mantra.
One does not interrupt the mantras of others;
one maintains an uninterrupted mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings;

And he proclaimed for them: "Now,
in establishing a maṇḍala,
it must be done during one of the three long months."
Within this month, one must obtain a waxing moon (śuklapakṣa) and not a waning moon (kṛṣṇapakṣa).
During the waxing moon, on either the first day or the fifteenth day,
one must further select an auspicious day.
A mandala may only be established when the auspicious stars and planets are favorable.
If one wishes to construct a maṇḍala outside of the three long months,
one should select an auspicious day and morning for its commencement.
Furthermore, one must select a pure location—
whether near a city wall, near the shore of a sea or river, facing out toward the ocean,
or at the ācārya’s own residence— and there construct the maṇḍala.
If one approaches a city wall and travels northeast,
a site that is neither too close nor too far may be used;
the ground to be used must be free of sand, stones, and debris.
Ashes, charcoal, excrement, soil, skulls,
and the like must all be removed so that the site is purified;
the ācārya then takes up residence there.
Alternatively, for seven days up to half a month, one should strictly maintain the site of the maṇḍala according to the ritual rules.
Then, using water that is free of insects and purified by the fivefold purification,
one should mix it with white sandalwood, camphor, and kumkuma incense within the water.
Forming the Great Mudrā of the Five Topknots, recite the mantra of the Great Wrathful Vidyārāja Yamāntaka eight thousand times.
Consecrate pure water with this and sprinkle it throughout the ten directions, the four intermediate points, above, and below, so that all are rendered pure.
The area of the altar where one resides shall measure sixteen cubits on each side, or twelve cubits, or eight cubits;
these are divided into three grades: superior, middling, and inferior.
The Wisdom of All-Wisdom has taught this maṇḍala rite.
If one seeks the security and stability of a kingdom and wishes to ascend the royal throne, the upper maṇḍala may be used.
If one seeks the increase of merit, fortune, and longevity, the middle maṇḍala may be used.
If one seeks all auspicious matters, one may use the lower mandala measuring eight cubits.
Furthermore, if one seeks a specific matter,
one should powder that maṇḍala.
One should excavate the site of the maṇḍala to a depth of two cubits.
If there are charcoal, ash, bricks, stones, tiles, rubble, bones, hair, snakes, insects, or similar things, the altar cannot be established;
one must seek out another auspicious location before proceeding with the construction.
One should not consider whether the mountain, wilderness, or riverbank presents any obstacles;
rather, one must simply observe with correct intention and a meticulous mind a place that is free of insects and pure.
Furthermore, the earth excavated from that site must be set aside to use only superior, pure soil for filling it back in.
Once filled, compact it firmly until it is level and full.
The pure earth used for filling must be mixed with the aforementioned five kinds of purified water.
The three-tiered maṇḍala may be constructed according to one’s preference.
Furthermore, drive one khaṇḍarohā-wood peg into each of the four corners of the maṇḍala.
Empower the pegs by reciting the mantra of the Wrathful Vidyārāja seven times.
Then, using five-colored thread, likewise recite the mantra of the Wrathful Vidyārāja seven times over it.
With these five-colored threads, encircle the form of this maṇḍala at its four directions;
the central position within the four directions is called the inner court.
Have the ācārya occupy the central position and recite the root mantra eight thousand times.
Having bound the Great Five-Knot Mudrā and completed the recitation of the mantra accordingly, [proceed].
That ācārya then steps outside the maṇḍala;
having circumambulated the maṇḍala once,
he sits facing east upon a grass mat.
With a sincere heart, prostrate to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Then, fasten the five-colored threads previously prepared to stakes at the four corners;
encircle the altar once with them to serve as the boundary cord.
Having mastered the ritual procedures, he should perform the recitation for one night.
That maṇḍala-ācārya, maintaining strict purity and fasting,
should act and apply his mind according to the fundamental ritual manual.
He causes the practitioner of the Mahāyāna to maintain the precepts according to the Dharma and perform ritual activities together for one night.
Furthermore, using five-colored powders, he recites the six-syllable heart-mantra.
Having consecrated that powder, place it within the maṇḍala;
furthermore, adorn and place banners and streamers at the four sides outside the altar.
Plant plantain trees and various fruit trees to form the gateway;
furthermore, have drums, musical instruments, conchs, and gongs produce their sounds in unison,
for these constitute auspicious sounds.
When the music and so forth had ceased,
he again briefly expounded the essential Dharma for the fourfold assembly.
Then, at the four directions of the maṇḍala...
Each shall read Mahāyāna sūtras:
those in the south shall read the *Bhagavatī Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*,
and those in the west shall read the *Ārya Candraprabha-samādhi Sūtra*.
In the north, one reads the Holy Avataṃsaka Sūtra;
in the east, one reads the Holy Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra.
When the Dharma Master has thus read these four sūtras, he shall...
The ācārya emerges from the maṇḍala and takes white sandalwood,
camphor, and kumuda— white fragrant substances—
and combines them with excellent flowers in one place.
Recite the root mantra while performing consecration (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
Scatter these incense and flowers throughout all parts of the maṇḍala.
The ācārya shall go outside for seven days and consume only clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
Furthermore, employ two to three persons who possess great merit,
have generated the bodhicitta, and maintain the precepts;
together they enter the maṇḍala, recite the root mantra, and perform self-protection.
Sprinkle this altar with five-colored powders.
The powder used should consist of the five precious substances such as gold and silver, made as fine as dust;
alternatively, the five colors of copper and other metals may also be used.
If a king or a person of great merit constructs this maṇḍala, they will certainly attain unsurpassed bodhi;
even those who rejoice in it shall likewise attain bodhi.
How much more so will other auspicious matters be accomplished without fail?
If, after the parinirvāṇa of Śākyamuni Tathāgata, there are sentient beings of meager merit in this degenerate age, [they shall likewise attain success].
"How could one be able to see or hear such a ritual procedure for the maṇḍala of great merit?
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī of Great Radiance,
for the sake of all suffering and impoverished sentient beings, [spoke thus].
A brief explanation of the maṇḍala ritual procedure:
use non-glutinous rice to make a fine powder, as delicate as flour,
and dye it five colors— blue, yellow, red, white, and black.
The Maṇḍala Ācārya himself binds the Great Seal of the Five Topknots (*pañcacīra-mahāmudrā*),
recites the root mantra to consecrate the colored powders, and then, at the southeast corner of the maṇḍala, the Ācārya...
Construct a fire altar according to the ritual rules.
The altar shall be two cubits wide and one cubit deep,
with its perimeter shaped like the petals of a lotus flower.
One should use *pālāśa* wood and the wood of the *śrīvṛkṣa* tree as moist fuel, each approximately one foot in length;
those that are both fresh and moist may be used.
Furthermore, one should employ the three substances of ghee, curd, and honey.
Moisten both ends of the firewood,
form the *vaseṣṭi* mudrā, recite the root mantra,
and invoke the deity of fire.

Furthermore, recite the one-syllable heart-root mantra eight hundred times and immediately perform the homa, which is the burning of the aforementioned wood. Next, carry out the ritual together with a skillful painter.
The Maṇḍala Ācārya, having donned the crown himself,
should visualize all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas within his heart as if they were present before his eyes. Then,
reciting the incense-offering mantra, he should join his palms in reverent salutation.
Having prostrated to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas and having prostrated to the Youth Mañjuśrī,
one should take the aforementioned five-colored powders and,
together with the painter, use them to powder the surface of the maṇḍala.
First, in the center of the maṇḍala, paint Śākyamuni Buddha,
seated upon a precious lion throne, endowed with all the major and minor marks, appearing as if in the Heaven of Pure Light (Śuddhāvāsakāyika) in the posture of preaching the Dharma.
The maṇḍala ācārya and his assistants who perform the painting should further recite the root mantra to effect their own protection.
Next, they should provide all the spirits and deities with their raw food offerings.
Outside this mandala, in the four directions and above and below,
one should distribute food and drink to satisfy them.
Furthermore, the ācārya must bathe his body and put on clean garments.
Perform the rite of protection near the fire altar.
Furthermore, take ghee and *kumuda* incense,
mix them together to form eight thousand small balls of food.
The Ācārya sits upon a seat of auspicious *śubha-kuśa* grass and recites the root mantra.
He performs a *homa* offering using the aforementioned ball of food (*piṇḍa*).
Furthermore, he uses white mustard seeds and recites the mantra of the wrathful deity Yamāntaka eight hundred times.
Consecrate mustard seeds and place them within a pure vessel.
Should there be any inauspicious or evil forms,
or any harsh sounds, or violent winds and rains;
If on a certain day there appear evil signs or various obstacles and difficulties,
simply perform seven rounds of homa using the aforementioned white mustard seeds, and all evils will naturally vanish.
If anyone encounters such obstacles and difficulties, [the same applies].
If one performs the homa five times using mustard seeds,
that person's obstacles and difficulties will fail to materialize and will instead be naturally subdued;
yet after a single kṣaṇa, they will again become possessed by a malevolent spirit.
Even if Śakra, Lord of the Devas, were to create obstacles for them,
they would nonetheless meet their end before long;
how much more so when humans, non-humans, or others with malicious intent create such obstacles?
The manner in which this wrathful vidyārāja Yamāntaka destroys fear is as follows:
furthermore, that reciter sits upon a seat of auspicious grass (kuśa).
Having recited the mantra of the wrathful king Yamantraka,
one should paint two pratyekabuddhas to the right of the image of Śākyamuni Buddha.
He sits in the full lotus posture upon a lotus throne.
Furthermore, in front of that Buddha's feet,
one should draw two great śrāvakas.
He assumes the posture of listening to the Dharma.
To his right, one should paint the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara,
adorned with all ornaments, seated upon a lotus throne like the full moon in autumn.
Holding a lotus in his left hand and making the gesture of granting boons (*varada-mudrā*) with his right,
to the right of that Avalokiteśvara,
one should paint the Honored One Pāṇḍaravāsinī.
With his left hand holding a lotus and his right hand performing a prostration toward the World-Honored One Śākyamuni,
he likewise sits upon a lotus, wears a jeweled crown, and has his right shoulder bared. In this manner,
one should further depict the Bodhisattva Tārā and the Bodhisattva Bhṛkuṭī, each seated according to the ritual rules.
Above that bodhisattva, one should further paint the Mother Prajñāpāramitā,
Buddhalocanā, and Uṣṇīṣavijayā,
as well as the sixteen great bodhisattvas.
Namely: Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva,
Gaganagañja Bodhisattva, and Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva Destroyer of Sin and the Bodhisattva Maitreya held white whisks in their hands and gazed up at the World-Honored One.
The Bodhisattva Pure Conduct and the Bodhisattva Stainless Banner likewise did so.
The Bodhisattva Subhavyūha, the Bodhisattva Candraprabha,
the Bodhisattva Vimalakīrti, the Bodhisattva Sarvarogāpagata,
the Bodhisattva Sarvadharmavaśavartirāja, and the Bodhisattva Lokagati.
The Bodhisattva Mahāmati and the Bodhisattva Dhāraṇīmati—
these sixteen great bodhisattvas were all fully adorned with perfect physical marks and features.
Furthermore, above that, one should again paint the wrathful Great Vidyārājas and the various Vidyārājas of the Lotus Family (*padmakula*).
They abide in their respective places, forming mudrās according to the ritual rules.
In the four directions of the maṇḍala, there are each vacant spaces.
One should merely paint lotus flowers and arrange the invocation of the worthy and holy ones therein.
Furthermore, to the right of Śākyamuni Buddha,
one should paint two pratyekabuddhas.
The first is named Khaṇḍa-mānava and the second is named Upalipta;
to the left of the Buddha, one should further depict two pratyekabuddhas.
One is named Cunda and the second is named Sthavira;
beneath the Buddha’s feet, one should draw two great śrāvakas:
Mahākāśyapa and Mahākātyāyana.
All mandalas have their doors facing east.
Furthermore, to the left of the Śrāvaka, one should depict the noble Vajrapāṇi,
blue like an utpala flower, adorned with all ornaments and perfect in his physical marks.
With his right hand he holds a fly-whisk, and with his left hand he strokes the crown of the head of the Wrathful Vidyārāja.
[There are also] the Vajramuṣṭi Vidyārāja, the Vajrāṅkuśa Vidyārāja,
the Vajrasphoṭa Vidyārāja, the Subāhu Vidyārāja, and the Vajrasena Vidyārāja.
Each sat according to their respective characteristics and insignia.
All the wrathful vidyārājas and vidyās, together with their retinues,
each formed mudrās according to the ritual rules.
To its left, one should further draw the mudrā of the Karma-vajra;
this is done likewise on all four sides of the maṇḍala.
Therein, the ācārya invites the vidyārāja and his retinue to dwell in retreat.
Upon that maṇḍala, one should further draw eight Uṣṇīṣa-vijaya Buddhas.
Their bodies are golden in color and emit radiance from every limb;
each forms a mudrā according to the ritual method, resembling the appearance of the Great Cakra-vikrāmin Vidyārāja.
The Buddha, adorned with perfect majesty, is to be beheld and contemplated; namely,
the Great Wheel Sovereign Victorious Uṣṇīṣa and the White Parasol Uṣṇīṣa.
The Uṣṇīṣavijayā Buddha-uṣṇīṣa, the Sarvatathāgatoṣṇīṣasitātapatrā Buddha-uṣṇīṣa,
the Raśmiprabhāsa Buddha-uṣṇīṣa, the Uṣṇīṣa-unnata, and so forth;
these should be painted at the gate on the left side of the aforementioned Pratyekabuddha.
On the right side outside the gate, paint a great bodhisattva named Lokottaracaryā (Transcending the World),
depicted with a topknot and a crown.
Holding a rosary in his right hand and a pure water flask (*kamaṇḍalu*) in his left,
he faces the door with an expression of either joy or frowning anger.
To the left of the door, one should paint a great Bodhisattva named Aparājita.
His appearance and demeanor are pure;
he also wears a crown.
His left hand holds a flask and staff, while his right hand holds a rosary and forms the mudrā of granting boons (*varada-mudrā*).
Facing the door, he likewise displays expressions of joy, anger, and frowning displeasure.
Furthermore, within the jeweled palace there is a wheel of Dharma (dharmacakra),
and beneath the wheel of Dharma is a lion throne (siṃhāsana).
Therein is a great bodhisattva, namely Mañjuśrī,
appearing in the form of a youth with a body the color of saffron (*kuṅkuma*),
his features pure and his countenance wearing an expression of both joy and wrath.
The left hand holds an *utpala* lotus, and the right hand performs the gesture of granting boons while holding an auspicious fruit (*śrīphala*).
His head has five topknots, he wears pearl necklaces,
and is clothed in celestial garments of *kauśika* silk.
With his right shoulder bared, his radiance shines everywhere;
all his ornaments take the form of a youth,
and he sits upon a lotus throne facing the entrance of the maṇḍala.
Behold the wrathful vidyārāja Yamāntaka;
on the right side of that bodhisattva, beneath a lotus seat,
one should further paint the wrathful vidyārāja Yamāntaka.
He assumes a form of great ferocity with radiance pervading his entire body;
he gazes up at the Bodhisattva with an expression as if receiving a command.
To the right, beneath a lotus, one should paint five Great Bodhisattvas.
They manifest in the form of the Śuddhāvāsakāyika devaputras, namely:
the Bodhisattva Vimala and the Bodhisattva Gambhīraśubha.
The Bodhisattva Viśuddha, the Bodhisattva Nivaraṇaviṣkambhin,
and the Bodhisattva Samantaprabha—
every one of them was like that in the Heaven of Utmost Purity and Radiance.
Throughout all places there were countless precious jewels and radiance;
various flowers were scattered as supreme adornments,
and furthermore, powders of five colors [were used].
Draw four gate-towers at the four sides of the maṇḍala.
In the northeast of the maṇḍala,
draw the Tathāgata King of Blossoming Flowers of the Upper Realm.
One should depict the Buddha’s body in a small scale, seated upon a lotus throne.
He should be fashioned in the likeness of Śākyamuni Buddha,
universally emitting light, sitting in the full lotus posture (paryaṅka), with his hands in the gesture of granting boons (varada-mudrā).
On the right side of that Buddha, paint the seal of Mahācakra-uṣṇīṣavijayā;
on the left side, the seal of Raśmijālinī, the seal of Buddhalocanā,
and the seal of Prajñāpāramitā.
The Seal of the Noble Avalokiteśvara for the Perfection of Wisdom (Prajñāpāramitā).
To the right of the Blessed One, one should paint Amitāyus,
gazing toward the Tathāgata with his hand in the gesture of granting boons (varada-mudrā).
Seated upon a lotus throne, he is universally radiant.
To the right of that Buddha, the seal of the robe and alms bowl is placed.
In this manner, there are successive intervals of empty space.
Furthermore, paint the Tathāgata Padmavikrāmin and the Lotus Seal;
on the right side, paint the Buddha-uṣṇīṣa Tejorāśi Seal and the Universal Radiance Seal, and to the right of that, place the Tathāgata Ratnaketu.
Seated upon a mountain of jewels, he assumes the posture of preaching the Dharma.
From that Buddha-body, various flames of light emerge,
manifesting as blue, green, and red, pervading everywhere with radiance.
To the left of that Buddha, the mudrās of Uṣṇīṣavijayā and the Turning of the Wheel of Dharma are depicted in colored powder,
both emitting brilliant light. To the left,
there are further depictions of a mendicant’s staff (khakkhara), a water flask (kamaṇḍalu), a rosary (akṣamālā), and a jeweled throne.
Apply these powders in sequence.
Furthermore, on the cheeks of the door, apply a three-pronged vajra with pervasive radiance.
At the feet of Mañjuśrī—
The five-crested great mudrā and the utpala flower mudrā are both endowed with radiance.
Such characteristics of the maṇḍala must all be complete.
Regarding all the entrances to the maṇḍala:
It is equally appropriate to place it either to the east or to the west.
Outside the maṇḍala, use fine powders of five colors to mark its four corners and the gate-towers of the four directions.
Outside the inner maṇḍala, leave a space of two cubits on each of the four sides.
Here, one should draw the Great Brahmā with four heads,
wearing white celestial garments.
With his right shoulder bared and a white cord draped across his armpit,
his body was golden in color and his topknot adorned with a golden crown;
in both his left and right hands, he held a flask and a staff.
Furthermore, on the right side, one should paint the deity *Ābhāsvara* (Extremely Radiant Purity),
whose body is golden in color and who wears a celestial garment of *kārṣāya* silk;
he displays the mudrā of meditative concentration and has a face suffused with a joyful expression.
With his hair tied in a topknot and wearing a crown, a white cord is draped across his armpits;
he sits in the full lotus posture with his right hand in the *varada-mudrā* (gesture of granting boons).
To his right is the Devaputra Akaniṣṭha.
Clad in a celestial garment of *kārṣāya*,
adorned with every ornament and bearing a joyful expression on his face,
he sits in the full lotus posture as if absorbed in meditative concentration.
With a white cord draped across his armpits and his right hand forming the mudrā of granting boons (*varadamudrā*),
he likewise successively delineated the deities of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, the Yāma heaven, the Tuṣita heaven, the Nirmāṇarati heaven, and the Paranirmitavaśavartin heaven with colored powder.
All the ritual characteristics are to be fully prepared in their proper sequence, one by one.
Furthermore, beneath the feet of Śakra, one should paint the four Great King devaputras: Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Virūḍhaka, Virūpākṣa, and Vaiśravaṇa.
Following the sequence and complete with the appropriate ritual characteristics,

one should paint in the southern direction the sons of the gods of the Heaven of Minor Light, the Heaven of Merit-Born, the Heaven Free from Heat, the Heaven of Good Vision, the Heaven of Good Appearance, and so forth.
Ensure that all their respective characteristics and postures are fully complete,
and likewise depict these various deities within the positions of the western sector.
Furthermore, on the exterior of the second tier of the maṇḍala:
On the four sides of the third tier maṇḍala,
draw the Four Heavenly Kings in sequence.
Enter through the maṇḍala gate from the north.
On the right side, paint the Lord of Wealth (Dhanada) and various treasure troves;
all their ornaments should be in accordance with the iconography of a yakṣa.
Following him on the right, paint in succession the yakṣa lords Ratnapāṇi and Pūrṇabhadra.
And there was Hārītī, the great yakṣiṇī,
cradling her beloved child and gazing up at the maṇḍala.
Furthermore, there were yakṣas such as Piṅgala, Bhiṣaṇa, and others, each positioned near their respective yakṣa seals.
Next is Varuṇa, holding a noose in his hand;
furthermore, one should paint the eight great nāga kings in the four directions:
the nāga king Nanda and the nāga king Upananda.
The Naga King Takṣaka, the Naga King Vāsuki, and others—
these should be depicted, arranged in two rows according to their respective order.
Next, one should depict the yakṣas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas.
One should further depict ṛṣis, āryas, yakṣas, piśācas,
garuḍas, humans, non-humans, and so forth,
as well as the supreme great medicinal herbs and the supreme maṇi jewels.
The greatest mountain, the greatest river, and the greatest city must all be the greatest and foremost;
in the southern region, one must likewise draw seven mahārājas along with their retinues.
In the southeast, one should paint the deity Agni (Fire God), who is of universal radiance;
he holds a water-pot, a staff,
and a rosary in his hands, wears a topknot and a crown, and is clothed in white celestial garments.
With the right shoulder bared, a white cord draped across the armpit, and a body of golden hue,
adorned with various ornaments and insignia,
he should likewise be depicted in two positions.
Outside this maṇḍala, Maheśvara rides upon a bull and holds a trident in his hand;
together with the goddess Umā, whose body is golden and adorned with various ornaments.
Next is the deity Kumāra, whose form is like that of a youth.
He rides upon a peacock, holds a spear in his hand, and has six heads with faces of a reddish hue.
He wears yellow garments, the attire of a celestial being (*devaputra*).
Holding a bell and a red banner in his left hand,
he is followed by the great host of the *Bhūṅgiriṭi* class,
appearing extremely emaciated.
The deities Nandikeśvara and Mahākāla,
along with the seven Mātṛs,
each adorned according to their respective insignia and ritual forms.
Furthermore, one should paint the eight devas, the seven ṛṣis, and Nārāyaṇa,
who has four arms holding a jewel-topped staff, a conch, and a sword,
and who rides upon a garuḍa adorned with all ornaments; one should also establish the eight lunar mansions.
The twenty-seven lunar mansions and the [nine] planets traverse the great earth.
Furthermore, eight minor planets are painted in their respective positions.
Additionally, the black and white phases of the fifteen days of the lunar month are depicted.
The twelve zodiac signs correspond to the twelve months of the year.
Four sisters ride upon a boat, while five brothers dwell within its waters.
As for the remaining classes [of beings], one should merely depict their seals.
All the worthy and noble ones are arranged in two rows.
The seats for the worthy and noble ones are set out in each of the three-layered maṇḍalas.
All three-layered maṇḍalas are made in the shape of a square.

The Buddha, the World-Honored One, is the foremost among all holy ones; to his right, one must paint Ārya Avalokiteśvara of the Lotus Family, and to his left, Vajrapāṇi of the Vajra Family—one must paint each of them.
Samantabhadra Bodhisattva and Mañjuśrīkumārabhūta—
these two must be depicted first in their proper sequence among the bodhisattvas; for the others,
one need only depict their hand-seals (mudrās).
Outside the inner maṇḍala, in the central area of the outer maṇḍala,
one should paint Mahābrahmā, the Lord of the Sahā World, and the Ābhāsvara-devas at the eastern position.
In the south, paint Akaniṣṭha Heaven;
for the four heavens of the formless realm, paint them in the state of formlessness.
In the north, [paint] Śakra, Lord of Devas, and Yama, Lord of Devas.
The Lord of Tuṣita Heaven, the Lord of Nirmāṇarati Heaven,
the Lord of Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, and the son of the gods from the Parīttābha Heaven—
each of these lords must be depicted.
For the remaining deities, one should merely depict their hand-seals (mudrā).
In the northern sector of the third tier maṇḍala,
one should depict Īśāna, the lord of the bhūtas, together with the homa.
On the second tier near the gate, depict the deity Kumāra and Mañjuśrī.
He rides upon a peacock and holds a spear in his hand;
his body is red in color, and he wears yellow garments with the right shoulder bared.
Holding a bell and a red banner in his right hand and assuming the appearance of a youth,
he gazes up at the maṇḍala.
To the east, one should paint the ṛṣi Mārkaṇḍeya as a bird.
As for the remaining paintings and mudrās:
in the southeast, paint the four sisters and the five brothers,
traveling together by boat upon the great ocean, as well as the Fire Deity (Agni).
In this manner, in the south, paint Pāñcika, the lord of the rākṣasas, who dwells on Mount Laṅkā.
Next, paint the deity Kumbhīra in the form of a yakṣa beneath a great tree; he is a bodhisattva.
Next, draw the King of Hungry Ghosts (Pretarāja) and the King of Piśācas in hideous forms;
for the others, merely draw their hand-seals (mudrās).
Next, in the south, draw the nāga kings Nanda and Upananda.
Furthermore, the Sun Deity is foremost among the *nakṣatras* and *grahas*.
To the west, one should depict the seer Kapilamuni and the non-Buddhist seer Nirgrantha.
All of them manifest the appearance of non-Buddhist practitioners (tīrthika).
Following their respective order, one should further draw their mudrās.
In the northwest, one should draw the Yakṣa King Vaiśravaṇa.
The Gandharva King Pañcaśikha,
the Kinnara King Mahādruma,
and the remaining painted seals.
Outside the fourth layer of the maṇḍala,
draw five-colored boundary paths together with the complete mudrās;
[this applies to] the four sides of the maṇḍala.
Paint the four gate-towers and the Four Great Heavenly Kings,
complete with all the seal-marks (mudrās) as previously described.
On the right side of the entrance, paint an utpala lotus flower.
On the left side, one should draw a lotus and a vajra-axe;
a sword, a spear, a trident, a jewel-staff, and a jewel-wheel;
and a *sārvastika* [crossed-vajra], a precious vase, a fish, and a conch shell.
The kamaṇḍalu, pure flask, banner, pennant, noose, bell,
sword, bow, arrow, golden mallet,
and various other such emblems, forms, and seal-marks are to be painted in all four directions.
Outside the square mandala, one should further draw four great mudrās.
Furthermore, in the northern direction of the maṇḍala,
one should place a five-pronged vajra that radiates light everywhere.
In the east, construct a small maṇḍala in the shape of a triangle,
placing a lotus that emits universal light.
In the south, construct a maṇḍala in the shape of a crescent moon.
Place the alms bowl with its pervasive radiance.
In the western maṇḍala, which has a circular form,
place a blue lotus together with its stem and leaves, with pervasive radiance.
Furthermore, there are four seals in the four corners.
In the northwest corner, a circular mandala is formed,
wherein a pāśa (noose) is placed, radiating light in all directions.
In the southwest corner, the maṇḍala is shaped like a crescent moon;
place a staff there, radiating light in all directions.
In the southeast corner, the maṇḍala is triangular in shape.
Place a battle-axe with universal radiance.
In the northeast, the maṇḍala is made square in shape;
place a sword with universal radiance.
Outside the gate of the maṇḍala, use five-colored powders to draw three seals—
upper, middle, and lower—
namely, the robe, the alms bowl, and the leather sandals, which are all-pervadingly radiant.
For the benefit of all sentient beings,
this is taught according to the ritual manual of this maṇḍala.
*The Great Vaipulya Sūtra of the Mañjuśrī-mūla-kalpa from the Bodhisattva-piṭaka*, Fascicle Five.
The Sixth Fascicle of the *Mañjuśrī-mūla-kalpa*, from the *Mahāvaipulya Bodhisattvapiṭaka Sūtra*.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Chao San Dafu, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial.

Translated by the Great Master Mingjiao, the Subject Tianxizai, by Imperial Decree. Chapter Two, Part Three: The Ritual of the Bodhisattva’s Manifestations. Furthermore, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī spoke as follows:
If a maṇḍala ācārya is to accept a disciple,
that person must have all six sense faculties complete and be endowed with the proper physical marks;
they may be a brāhmaṇa, kṣatriya, vaiśya, or śūdra.
Those who have resolved to attain bodhicitta and practice the Mahāyāna path without seeking inferior fruits;

and other such ugly beasts, whether two-legged or four-legged,
as well as hear them making sounds.
If the practitioner naturally realizes that the altar ritual has not been perfected and the sought-after objective is not accomplished,
the reciter-ācārya must re-establish the pure altar and perform the rite once again.
In this manner, continue until the seventh repetition.
Even if the practitioner has committed the five heinous crimes,
upon reaching the seventh repetition, they will certainly attain accomplishment.
Once the maṇḍala has been completed,
have the aforementioned young girl sit upon a seat of auspicious grass (kuśa), facing either east or north.
The ācārya shall recite mantras and provide protection.
He shall instruct the young girl to maintain a vegetarian diet and observe the fast,
and then he shall teach her the aforementioned tūla-thread ritual.
Have them spin it into cotton thread,
weighing one *liang*, three *liang*, five *liang*, eight *liang*, up to sixteen *liang*.
It must be of the highest quality, even, and the weight must be precisely determined.
If it is for the superior level of altar ritual, sixteen *liang*;
for the middle level, eight *liang*;
and for the inferior level, from five *liang* down to one *liang*.
If one performs rites of subjugation, they will vary according to one's own power and the circumstances of the moment;
if this mandala is accomplished,
even past karmic obstructions from previous lives will be spontaneously eliminated in an instant.
Take the cotton thread previously spun by the maiden and place it in a clean vessel;
focus the mind single-pointedly upon it without allowing other objects to arise as conditions.
Then, use camphor, white sandalwood, and saffron.
Place them together in a clean vessel and wrap them with cotton thread.
Offer *mālikā* flowers and *campaka* flowers as an offering to effect protection.
When reciting mantras and performing any ritual acts, one must not be distracted.
All utensils used must be pure and free from insects or ants.
