The Great Master Mingjiao, the Subject Tianxi-zai, respectfully translated by imperial decree. Chapter Four, Part Two: The Ritual Procedures for the Superior Grade of Painted Images. Furthermore, once the method for the ritual cord has been completed, one seeks out those who shall create the painted image.
The person he employs must have a handsome appearance;
they should be neither too fat nor too thin, free from illness and suffering,
neither aged nor frail, and neither wicked nor ugly.
One who breathes without coarse laboredness, is free from the affliction of sores and scabs,
possesses all sense faculties, and has a dignified and handsome appearance; furthermore, one whose mind is gentle and supple, who delights in practicing virtuous deeds,
and whose wisdom is penetrating and skillful in the highest degree— such a person may be commissioned to paint the scroll.
If one obtains such a person to create this painted image, the benefit will be supreme.
Furthermore, there are three grades of distinction for this painted image:
the superior grade of painted image yields superior benefits and merit.
A painting of medium quality yields medium benefit;
a painting of inferior quality yields inferior benefit.
If one obtains the person who originally commissioned the painting...
The labor required and its price—whether it be much or little—must not be treated with fear or stinginess;
one should have the work performed according to the price.
If one lacks personal wealth, one should seek it out through skillful means.
One should cause them to paint the scroll so that it will certainly be accomplished;
once the scroll image is accomplished, its merit is as if it were fully realized,
and one should employ the most supreme and excellent incense and flowers.
Furthermore, he provides every kind of offering— delightful to humans and devas—
including rare curiosities, precious vessels, food, drink, clothing, bedding, and medicinal requisites,
thereby enabling all sentient beings to obtain great benefit through the authentic awakening and authentic teaching.
Furthermore, the ācārya must first cause the person who is to create the paṭa to receive the upavāsa precepts.
Moreover, one must select an auspicious day;
it must be one of the three long months, during the bright fortnight, and on a day of the waxing moon.
One may have a paṭa created when the stars and planetary positions are auspicious;
if a specific month is required, it must be the second or third month,
during a time of spring harmony when flowers are in full bloom and fragrant.
At the moment the sun first rises, one should immediately have the materials for making the scroll produced;
all items used for the construction, such as the cloth and the threads,
must be washed together with cow dung, pure earth, and water.
Having washed it, wash it again with five kinds of pure water free from insects.
In a quiet place, perform the ritual sprinkling of purification using sandalwood and *kunkuma* perfumed water.
Place the previously prepared scroll and ritual implements here.
Furthermore, offer incense and flowers with a sincere mind.
The *ācārya* shall bathe to become pure and don fresh, clean robes.
Wearing a crown and dressed in white, partaking of sandalwood, kunkuma, camphor, and other fragrances,
free from thoughts of hunger and thirst and with a heart full of joy,
one should hold white mustard seeds and recite the mantra eight hundred times, then cast the seeds toward the four cardinal directions, the four intermediate directions, above, and below.
Furthermore, by binding the Great Seal of the Five Topknots (*pañca-śikhā-mahāmudrā*) and holding mustard seeds,
one performs empowerment over the crown of the person who creates the cloth painting (*paṭa*), thereby obtaining great protection.
If it is a superior-quality painting, it shall be four cubits wide and eight cubits long.
The medium-quality painting is two cubits wide and five cubits long.
The inferior-quality painting is one *buddha-cubit* wide and three and a half cubits long.
As for the *buddha-cubit*, it is the cubit of one who is eight feet tall; that is, one cubit constitutes a *buddha-cubit*.
This is the fixed measurement for the three grades of paṭas.
Furthermore, the superior grade of paṭa can accomplish the highest matters of entering the state of sainthood and so forth.
The middling grade of paṭa is for seeking the supreme rank after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
Those who seek the supreme merit shall achieve accomplishment in both;
those of inferior capacity who seek the happiness of humans and devas, wealth, treasures, and precious gems,
as well as the rites of subjugation, shall likewise achieve accomplishment in all.

If one practices according to this dharma, one will certainly achieve accomplishment; even if one does not practice according to this dharma, one will not achieve accomplishment even if one were as powerful as the Lord of Devas.
If one follows and practices according to the dharma, even a person of lowly station may achieve accomplishment.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have proclaimed the Dharma teachings and the practices of mantras and secrets as causes for the enlightenment of all sentient beings.
If a person resolves their mind upon these mantra teachings and upholds them, [they shall attain the fruit].
There is no maṇḍala, whether mundane or supramundane, that this person will not accomplish;
before long, they shall attain great enlightenment.
If this dharma were not beneficial for the practitioner of bodhi, [it would not be so].
The Buddha did not proclaim it for them.
Furthermore, regarding the ritual rules for the painted image (*paṭa*) as taught by the youth Mañjuśrī,
there is also a sequential order of time limits within this.
If one intends to create this painting, one should do so with a focused mind;
it may be completed in five days, eight days, or sixteen days.
If a person applies themselves single-mindedly, it can be completed in a single day and night.
This is called the supreme accomplishment, which brings about immense benefit.
If that practitioner voids urine or excrement,
they must remain more than a hundred paces away from the site of the painting.
When that task is completed, one should bathe with pure water and put on fresh, clean garments.
Furthermore, one should apply white sandalwood paste to the body, as well as to the hands and feet.
One must then focus the mind and concentrate the will.
The cloth for the banner (paṭa) must be finely woven and firm, prepared according to the Dharma; furthermore, its dimensions must be appropriate and measured correctly, with no excess or deficiency.
Any remaining threads should be tied and knotted in accordance with the Dharma.
Hang it level and straight using a bamboo pole.
Once it has been completed on an auspicious day during the waxing moon,
ensure that the payment is made in full without any deficiency.
He should cause them to settle their minds and enjoy [the benefits] according to the Dharma.
The Ācārya shall then install this painted image in a pure place according to the ritual, and perform consecration and offerings with the finest incense and flowers.
This protection of oneself, as well as of the thread and the cloth-painting,
is proclaimed by the mantra of the Greatly Powerful Mañjuśrī;
it was likewise spoken by the Buddhas of the past.
I shall now likewise proclaim for you such things as all mantra practices and the characteristics of mantras,
which possess great diligence and great power.
They are able to perform and accomplish various Buddha-works,
and further, they are able to rescue and deliver the deluded and confused sentient beings of Jambudvīpa who hold wrong views,
are inverted in their understanding, and reject the sacred teachings.
May they attain liberation from the darkness of saṃsāra.
If there are those who have faith and delight in mantras,
who receive and uphold them according to the Dharma, and who, generating great courage and practicing great diligence, seek supreme enlightenment;
It is certain that they will achieve success as the Buddha has taught.
If there are sentient beings who do not believe,
they will be unable to plant those seeds of bodhi.
For example, just as salt-infused soil cannot produce the sprouts of the hundred grains even if their seeds are gathered there,
faith is the root of all virtues and can give birth to the seeds of omniscience.
If one has faith, understanding, and maintains this mantra, all that is sought shall be accomplished.
If that ācārya seeks to have it painted, he shall have it depicted upon a cloth painting (paṭa).
One must also personally understand the requirements for preparing the painting materials.
The artist must possess the highest skill and be endowed with all the necessary characteristics;
they should be gentle, compassionate, and of dignified appearance.
Having cleared them of all faults, they shall receive the precepts again.
The consecration is to be performed according to the same ritual procedures as those for creating a painted banner (*paṭa*).
All pigments used must be of superior quality, radiant and pure, and free from dust and impurities.
Then, using incense such as camphor, white sandalwood, and *kunkuma*,
one should fumigate the colors and empower them by reciting the mantra eight hundred times.
Furthermore, [one should use] *nāgapuṣpa* and *bhaṇḍīraka* flowers.
Scatter upon the cloth *vākula* flowers,
rain-flowers (*varṣābhū*), *dhātuṣkārī* flowers, *mālīka* flowers,
*kusuma* flowers, and so forth.
Have the painter sit facing east upon a seat of *śrīparṇa* grass,
single-mindedly recollecting all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas to seek their empowerment;
he should then proceed with meticulous attention and a refined mind.
Do not grow weary while painting the meritorious qualities;
first paint Śākyamuni Buddha,
ensuring that all his marks are fully complete.
He possesses the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics;
he sits upon a precious lotus flower with a blazing halo, his countenance serene and joyful, his radiance pervading his entire body as he assumes the posture of preaching the Dharma.
The lotus upon which he sits has lapis lazuli for its stem.
Beneath the lotus is a great pond,
within which dwell two dragon kings.
One was named Nanda and the other was named Upananda.
With their left hands they held lotus stalks, and with their right hands they prostrated themselves at the feet of the Tathāgata, gazing up in reverence;
they were half human in appearance and half the form of snakes.
The body is white in color and endowed with all manner of ornaments.
Furthermore, that lotus pond abounds with lotuses, lotus leaves, aquatic creatures, and birds;
they are adorned with auspicious marks and are exquisitely beautiful and upright.
Furthermore, from the stalks of the lotus upon which that Tathāgata sits,
extending upward and downward and all around, emerge countless lotuses, arranged in successive tiers of varying heights,
each finding its proper place. To the left of the World-Honored One, there are eight great bodhisattvas, each seated upon a lotus throne.
First is the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī,
white as a lotus, or the color of kumkuma, or golden in hue;
he has the appearance of a youth with five topknots upon his head.
Fully adorned, upright and exquisite,
he holds an *utpala* flower in his left hand and pays homage to the Tathāgata with his right.
His face bears an expression of both joy and anger, his body is encircled by a halo, and he sits in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*).
The second is the noble Bodhisattva Padmacandraprabha, who also appears in the form of a youth;
the third is Padmavasu; and the fourth is Padmottara.
The Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin;
fifth, the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha;
sixth, the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha.
The seventh was the Bodhisattva Priceless;
the eighth was the Bodhisattva Wondrous Eye-Mind.
All these bodhisattvas appeared in the form of youths.
Each was perfectly adorned.
To the right of that Buddha, there were eight great bodhisattvas, fully arrayed with various ornaments;
the first, Maitreya Bodhisattva, sat closest to the Buddha.
He manifests the appearance of a Brahmā, wearing a jewel crown upon his head;
his body is of true golden color, clad in red robes and further draped in a red celestial garment;
his physical form is upright and majestic, endowed with the three types of insignia.
Holding a water flask in his left hand with a staff slung over his shoulder, and a black antelope skin draped across it,
he grasps a rosary in his right hand and pays homage to the Tathāgata;
gazing up at the World-Honored One, his mind remains as if in meditative concentration.
The second is the holy Samantabhadra Bodhisattva of the Lotus Family.
His body is purple-green in color and possesses all the marks of adornment.
His left hand holds a wish-fulfilling *maṇi* jewel.
His right hand holds a *śrīvatsa* fruit and performs the gesture of bestowing boons (*varada-mudrā*).

The third is the Noble Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, whose body is like the color of the autumn moon and who is adorned with all ornaments; he wears a jeweled crown and a white robe draped over his shoulders.
Upon the crown of the head, one further visualizes the emanated Amitāyus Buddha sitting upright and majestic;

his left hand holds a lotus flower, his right hand performs the mudrā of granting boons (*varada-mudrā*), and his entire body radiates light—thus one should perform the visualization as described for the heart.
The fourth is the noble Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi.
His body is golden in color and adorned with all ornaments;
his left hand holds a vajra, and his right hand is in the mudrā of granting boons while holding a fruit.
His body was adorned with necklaces and he wore a jeweled crown;
the crown emitted radiance and was draped with strings of pearls across his armpits.
He was clad in white garments and further wrapped in a white ascetic robe.
With his right shoulder bared like Avalokiteśvara;
fifth is the Great Holy Being Padmapāṇi Bodhisattva;
sixth is Sumati Bodhisattva.
The seventh is Samantaprabhāgarbha Bodhisattva,
and the eighth is Pāpavināśana Bodhisattva;
thus, each of those bodhisattvas holds a scripture and fruit in their hands.
Adorned with all the marks of excellence and arrayed in celestial robes,
above that bodhisattva one should further paint eight pratyekabuddhas,
depicted in the form of monks and wearing saffron-colored garments.
Seated in the full lotus posture upon a precious lotus flower,
he possesses the auspicious marks on his face like that of a great man;
his entire body radiates light, and his hands are held in the gesture of scattering flowers.
One should paint the *samalī* flower, the *puṣparāga* flower, the *uśīraka* flower, the *nāgapuṣpa* flower, and the *punnāga* flower,
scattering each one everywhere upon the cloth.
Furthermore, to the left of Śākyamuni Buddha, above the noble Mañjuśrī...
Paint the palaces and towers of Mount Sumeru,
adorned with countless exquisite jewels and covered everywhere with *utpala* flowers;
upon that mountain, further paint the eight World-Honored Buddhas.
The first is the Tathāgata Ratnaśikhin.
Upon his crown are various precious jewels, such as lapis lazuli, red lotus gems, indranīla, mahānīla, and ratnagarbha.
These great jewels radiate light everywhere, like the rising sun.
That Buddha’s body was clad in yellow robes,
with his right shoulder bared; he sat in the full lotus posture,
endowed with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs of excellence.
All his ornaments manifest the appearance of preaching the Dharma.
The second Tathāgata, King of Blossoming Flowers,
has a body of true golden color and emits great precious light.
Scattering flowers that please the mind, such as *nāgavakula* and other blossoms,
he sits in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*) and contemplates the noble Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva and the third Tathāgata, Śaḷendrarāja.
His body is the color of a golden lotus and he displays the mudrā of preaching the Dharma.
Fourth is the Tathāgata Subhanetra;
fifth is the Tathāgata Utpalasaṃhita.
The sixth is the Tathāgata Samantaprabhāsa; the seventh is the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabharāja;
the eighth is the Tathāgata Sarvaduḥkhapraśamanarāja.
These eight Buddhas are all universally golden in color.
He gazed upon Śākyamuni Tathāgata,
whose hands were in the gesture of fearlessness; moreover, from the sky above the Tathāgata,
clouds rained down various fragrant flowers.
In the two corners of the painting, depict the two Śuddhāvāsakāyika devaputras abiding in the void,
prostrating before the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas.
As for the eight pratyekabuddhas mentioned previously:
Namely: the Khaṇḍa pratyekabuddha, the Manana pratyekabuddha,
the Caṇḍana pratyekabuddha, the Upalipta pratyekabuddha,
the Śikṣita pratyekabuddha, and the Siddhārthaka pratyekabuddha.
After the pratyekabuddha Nimi, paint another pratyekabuddha, Sūnimi;
and following the pratyekabuddhas, further depict the eight great śrāvaka elders, namely the elder Śāriputra and the elder Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
The Venerable Mahākāśyapa, the Venerable Subhūti,
the Venerable Rāhula, the Venerable Nanda,
the Venerable Panthaka, and the Venerable Kapphiṇa.
These śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas,
endowed with all the marks of excellence and majestic in their merit,
joined their palms in reverent devotion and gazed up at the World-Honored One.
Furthermore, on the face of Śākyamuni Buddha,
separately depict two Śuddhāvāsakāyika devaputras,
their bodies adorned with flower garlands and garments, and their hands holding precious parasols.
With pearl necklaces, jeweled garlands, lotuses,
and exquisite ornaments such as great sapphires,
they covered the crown of the head of Śākyamuni Tathāgata.
Furthermore, beneath the Buddha’s feet there is a lotus pond;
it should be painted near Mañjuśrī and the Nāga kings Upananda and Nanda.
A single mountain of jewels rises from the lotus pond;
it has jeweled cliffs surrounded by jewel trees,
upon which hang coral vines and the flowers and fruits of the grasses and trees.
All are adorned with rare jewels.
A great ṛṣi dwells upon this mountain; on its northern side, the wrathful vidyārāja Yamāntaka is depicted with a most fierce and terrible appearance.
His right hand holds a noose and his left hand holds a staff;
his face wears a frown and his belly is vast and expansive;
his body is the color of ink, comparable to a black cloud.
His beard and hair are both long and yellowish-red;
both eyes are red, and his ten fingernails are long.
He is adorned with all ornaments and wears a garment of tiger skin.
Beholding Mañjuśrī in the posture of receiving a command,
his entire body blazing with light capable of destroying all obstacles and difficulties,
he sat upon a great rock at the foot of the mountain.
Furthermore, one should depict the practitioner near Nanda the Nāga King,
drawn according to his physical appearance and attire,
with his right knee touching the ground and his hand holding an incense burner.
To the right of the feet of the World-Honored One Śākyamuni,
a great mountain of jewels emerges from a lotus pond;
its magnificent adornments are likewise as described for the previous mountain.
On the northern face of the mountain, one should also paint a wrathful vidyārāja.
Furthermore, below the noble Avalokiteśvara,
one should again depict that mountain as the color of a red lotus.
It is also adorned with precious jewels,
with peaks made of lapis lazuli.
The Holy Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva transforms himself into the Holy Tārā Bodhisattva.
Dwelling on this mountain peak, his body is of a true golden color;
he is neither fat nor thin, neither old nor young.
He wears various garments, most notably a supreme red celestial robe.
She assumes the form of a woman, adorned with various ornaments;
her left hand holds an *utpala* flower, and her right hand makes the gesture of granting boons (*varada-mudrā*).
Her face displays an expression of both joy and anger, and she sits in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*).
Beholding the Noble Avalokiteśvara, whose entire body is radiant with light,
one should further depict a dragon-flower tree (*nāgapuṣpa*) upon a lapis lazuli peak in front of him;
its flowers are exquisite and blooming across the tree, with branches and leaves hanging down on all four sides.
Upon the crown of the Bodhisattva’s head, it is like a parasol;
before the Bodhisattva, it is adorned with the radiance of various precious jewels.
This Bodhisattva is able to shatter all obstacles and difficulties, and sever all fears.
If one who maintains and recites this [mantra] receives protection from her,
she manifests in the form of a celestial maiden; she is also a transformation of the Buddha,
capable of bestowing upon all sentient beings whatever they seek, so that all their aspirations are fully satisfied.
Furthermore, she is the mother of the youth Mañjuśrī;
for the benefit of all sentient beings,
one should also depict the wrathful vidyārāja upon this mountain.
The Buddhas have declared that this Great Vidyārājñī possesses great efficacy and great power;
she is endowed with great ferocity and manifests great wrath.
It can destroy all obstacles and difficulties.
If there are stubborn sentient beings who slander the holy teachings,
it can skillfully subdue them and cause them to believe and accept [the Dharma].
If there are those who uphold and recite it, they shall receive protection;
yet there are also those who slander the mantra, treat the Triple Gem with contempt,
and commit all manner of sinful deeds.
Whether they dwell in the celestial realms, reside upon the earth,
or inhabit the subterranean regions, all shall be tamed and made to follow and train according to this painted image;
ensure that its four sides, four corners, and the top and bottom are perfectly aligned and upright.
On the lower edge of the painting, near the border, one should depict the Great Ocean Nāga King.
His form is like that of a human, his body is white in color, and he is dignified and exquisite.
He is adorned with mani-jewels upon his body, and his entire person radiates light.
Upon his topknot he wears seven dragon heads;
possessing great merit and performing great diligence,
he is named Ānanda and is also called the Great Dragon.
Facing north with palms joined, gaze up at the Tathāgata.
To fulfill the Buddha’s instructions for benefiting all sentient beings in the world and destroying all obstacles and difficulties,
this ritual procedure for the painting-scroll is the most supreme.
I now briefly explain what the Tathāgatas of the past taught according to the capacities of beings.
Any person who upholds and recites this shall obtain boundless merit;
furthermore, even the grave sins committed over millions of kalpas [shall be purified].
In a single instant, they will swiftly be dissolved.
Even those who have committed the ten evil deeds, the five heinous crimes, violated the precepts, or wrought evil—
those who wander through the miserable realms as beings of lowly status— [shall be purified].
If one has never upheld or rejoiced in the Dharma,
yet encounters this painting and rejoices while gazing upon it,
their transgressions will be swiftly extinguished in a single kṣaṇa.
How much more so for one who recites it;
such a person will constantly achieve accomplishment in this sublime Dharma of the mantra.
Furthermore, if there were someone who, for ten million eons (*koṭi-kalpa*), made offerings to all the Buddhas—
The merit obtained is immeasurable;
likewise, the merit of both the practitioner who recites the mantra and the one who possesses the painted scroll is also immeasurable.
Furthermore, if there is a person who offers incense, flowers, food,
and drink as an offering to immeasurable Buddhas, bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River.
The merit and fruit obtained by that person are immeasurable.
If one recites, studies, and makes offerings to this mantra ritual,
the merit obtained shall likewise be immeasurable.
Furthermore, if there is a disciple who has received the teachings,
they may accomplish all *mantra* practices before this painting,
seeking the realization of those Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Great Bodhisattvas.
That person will certainly and swiftly attain accomplishment.
Chapter Five: The Ritual Procedures for the Medium-Sized Cloth Paintings. At that time, the World-Honored One, Śākyamuni Buddha...
Observing that the entire great assembly was eager and desirous to hear,
he addressed the youth Mañjuśrī, saying:
"I shall explain for you all the ritual rules for the medium-sized painted image."
Listen now attentively, contemplate it well, and do not forget it.
Mañjuśrī, suppose a skilled artisan were commissioned to create cotton threads and to prepare a painted cloth image.
The ritual procedures for empowerment and the various rules are all as previously explained in the superior [section].
Now, regarding the measurements and proportions of the cloth paintings (paṭa) belonging to this intermediate [category]:
Furthermore, there are slight differences in the ritual protocols maintained by those Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Śrāvakas.
Now, on the thangka, one should first paint the deity Pure Light (Śuddhaprabhā), with a ground made of crystal (*sphatika*).
It is universally adorned with necklaces of white pearls;
it is vast, level, and upright, being the most exquisite and supreme.
Within this celestial hall, the World-Honored One Śākyamuni Buddha is depicted.
Seated upon a lion throne made of the seven precious gems,
fully adorned with all the primary and secondary marks,
he manifests the appearance of preaching the Dharma before those humans and devas.
To the right of the Buddha, one should paint the noble Mañjuśrī.
His body is the color of a red lotus, or the color of *kunkuma*, or like the color of the sun.
An *utpala* flower hangs from his left shoulder; he has five topknots and the appearance of a youth.
With a joyful expression on his face, he stands with palms joined in reverence;
seated or standing with his right knee raised, he gazes up at the World-Honored One.
Furthermore, to the left of the World-Honored One, one should depict the noble Avalokiteśvara, whose face is like the full moon of autumn.
The various marks and ornaments are as previously described;
furthermore, add the hand-holding white fly-whisk fanning the body of the World-Honored One.
Next, paint the Bodhisattva Maitreya and the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra.
The Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the Great-Minded Bodhisattvas,
the Bodhisattva Sumati, the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja,
and the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin were all adorned individually, just like the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.
Furthermore, above that, the Bodhisattva should paint eight Buddha-Bhagavāns,
namely: the Tathāgata Padmottara-rāja, the Tathāgata Ratna-śikhin,
the Tathāgata Viśvabhū, and the Tathāgata Kakutsunda.
The Tathāgata Suvarṇarṣabha, the Tathāgata Kāśyapa,
the Tathāgata Sunetra, and the Tathāgata Krakucchanda—
all these Tathāgatas wear robes of light crimson.

One will receive protection in all undertakings.
If one binds the Great Seal of the Five Topknots and recites one *vyākṣa*,
there is no requested matter that shall not be accomplished.
If one uses cow dung to purify the ground and water free of insects for bathing the body,
as well as for sprinkling upon the altar site,
both the practitioner and all implements used shall become pure and clean.
One must not use stagnant water that does not flow or foul water.
Nor should one engage in frivolous talk regarding sentient beings.
Furthermore, one must perform visualization of oneself.
It is suffering, empty, impermanent, and non-self;
it has no master, no ruler, no savior, and no refuge.
Transmigration knows no end, and one harbors deep thoughts of suffering.
It is like entering deep water with single-minded concentration;
if one departs from this visualization, it is like a ruddy sheldrake separated from its mate, causing constant and increasing suffering.
Furthermore, that reciter must constantly maintain this visualization.
The realm of the Buddhas is a lotus pond of the seven treasures,
filled with blue, yellow, red, and white lotuses and lotus leaves in full bloom.
The four sides of the pond are adorned with various kinds of ornaments.
The World-Honored One sat upon that lion throne,
his golden radiance and the marks and signs of perfection all fully complete.
To the right of the Buddha was the noble Mañjuśrī.
Adorned with all the marks [of a Buddha], seated upon a lotus throne and holding a white fly-whisk,
visualize him as either sitting or standing, and either red, white, or golden in color.
To the left of that Buddha is the noble Avalokiteśvara.
Like the moonlight of the mid-autumn night, he holds a white fly-whisk in his hand.
Furthermore, there are eight bodhisattvas:
Maitreya, Samantabhadra, Kṣitigarbha, and Ākāśagarbha.
Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, Aparājita, Vajrapāṇi, and Ratnapāṇi—these, together with the aforementioned, constitute the ten bodhisattvas on the right side. There are eight pratyekabuddhas:
the pratyekabuddha Jñānagupta and the pratyekabuddha Kṣemagupta.
Ketu Pratyekabuddha, Suketu Pratyekabuddha,
Śvetaketu Pratyekabuddha, R̥ṣṭa Pratyekabuddha,
Upār̥ṣṭa Pratyekabuddha, and Nimi Pratyekabuddha.
And the eight great śrāvakas:
Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Śāriputra, Gavāmpati, and Piṇḍola.
Pūrṇa, Pilindavatsa, Rāhula, Mahākāśyapa,
and Ānanda— thus they visualized. Furthermore,
nearby that great assembly of śrāvakas was an infinite multitude of bhikṣus.
Near the pratyekabuddhas were infinite assemblies of pratyekabuddhas;
near the eight great bodhisattvas were infinite assemblies of bodhisattvas;
and so on, until the great assembly filled the entire realm of empty space.
Having performed such visualization,
the reciter further contemplates himself within the waters of the pond, with the water reaching his navel.
With various kinds of celestial and terrestrial flowers—
māndārava flowers, mahāmāndārava flowers,
dhatuṣkāri flowers, and rain-flowers.
Indīvara flowers, lotus flowers, and great lotus flowers—
such flowers piled up like Mount Sumeru,
as well as various banners, streamers, precious canopies, celestial garments, and exquisite incense.
They lit hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of lamps to make offerings to all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas,
while simultaneously providing food and making offerings to all sentient beings.
Furthermore, one should visualize the World-Honored One emitting white light from the tuft of hair between his eyebrows, illuminating all sentient beings.
If a practitioner recites [the mantra] while performing this meditative visualization according to the ritual procedures, they shall achieve success.
Before long, one will achieve the great fruit of Bodhi.
Furthermore, the Buddha taught this method of contemplative practice for the benefit of all sentient beings.
It is the foremost of the supreme practices for the practitioner of recitation (*jāpaka*).

Furthermore, as the Buddha taught, it contains the three types of maṇḍalas, the three categories of methods for accomplishment (*sādhanavidhi*), and the ritual procedures for the three kinds of painted banners (*paṭa*).
That practitioner, following the sequence of the ritual according to the dharma,
should carefully employ a pure mind to perform the visualization;
this will enable them to sever all root and secondary afflictions.
Thereafter, one offers arghya water to dismiss the noble ones and sages.
One then visualizes oneself emerging from the water;
only then is the practice of contemplation complete.
You who recite mantras should constantly practice them so that they are never forgotten.
If you wish to perform the recitation according to the ritual procedures as previously described,
you should again arrange the painted image in a pure place.
Perform the delimitation of the boundary (*sīmābandha*), the invocation (*āvāhana*), the offerings (*pūjā*), and the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
Conduct the *homā* ritual to seek their protection exactly as previously described.
Furthermore, within this present rite, one should additionally offer praises to the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and holy ones (*ārya*).
If one wishes to relieve oneself of excrement or urine, one should go to a secluded place away from the ritual site where there is no wind.
During the day, face east; at night, face south.
Furthermore, one must not contemplate matters such as the Buddha-dharma.
When such matters have been concluded in an unclean place,
wash your hands with pure earth and insect-free pure water,
and recite the aforementioned mantra thirty times.
Recite [the mantra] seven times while urinating.
Or, having spat out mucus or saliva, go neither too near nor too far from the altar;
one must also wash both hands thoroughly.
However, when washing one's feet every day,
one should first wash the right foot and afterwards the left foot;
the two feet must not touch each other.
Nevertheless, one purifies by means of fragrant ointments;
furthermore, there are five kinds of purity for the reciter:
first, purity of physical action (*kāyakarman*).
Second is the purity of verbal action;
third is the purity of mental action;
fourth is the purity of practicing reality.
The fifth discourse explains the Dharma of true purity.
Furthermore, one is able to penetrate the subtle, supreme, and most profound Dharma,
remaining far removed from killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct.
Lying, harsh speech, and divisive talk;
greed, hatred, and wrong views; violating the precepts and practicing what is contrary to the Dharma;
or if one commits unrighteous acts such as killing and stealing.
Those who, out of ignorance and false views,
slander and revile the True Dharma will fall for eternal kalpas into the realm of Yama as animals or hungry ghosts;
or they shall enter the Black Rope, Reviving, and other hells, up to the Great Avīci Hell, where they undergo various kinds of great suffering.
Even if one has obtained a human body, if the sense faculties are incomplete and one is deluded, ignorant, and dull-witted,
how could one possibly accomplish the supreme Dharma? Therefore,
those who maintain the recitation [should be diligent].
Staying far away from all evils and drawing near to virtuous friends,
one who diligently practices the various mantras according to the Dharma will certainly attain accomplishment in the supreme teaching.
Furthermore, this ritual manual has superior, middling, and inferior [versions].
If the practitioner follows each ritual procedure according to its respective manual and performs the rite with a sincere mind,
the ritual matters will harmonize and the person and the dharma will be fully perfected.
All that one seeks shall be accomplished.
Furthermore, the fruits achieved through the practice of mantra depend entirely upon the ritual manual (*vidhi*);
when the ritual manual is perfected, the objective is realized.
Thus, the mantras possess power and merit far exceeding the ordinary;
whatever one desires or seeks will certainly be accomplished.
Nevertheless, even if one recites the mantras, if the ritual procedures are deficient or the practice is inconsistent with the rules, [the result will not be achieved].
In that case, the mantra-dharma would lack its superior efficacy;
if one seeks the great fruit, it will certainly not be accomplished.
Furthermore, regarding these three grades of ritual procedures:
Each must be employed according to its respective rite and may not be used interchangeably;
if one employs a medium-grade ritual within a superior-grade [rite],
or a superior-grade method within a medium-grade [rite].
If one practices a middling matter within an inferior grade,
or practices a superior-grade dharma within an inferior grade—
in such ways, there is a mutual intermingling of the three grades.
Whatever one seeks will not be accomplished.
If that practitioner begins the ritual procedure,
performing the rites according to the Dharma and executing the ritual according to the prescribed form with a mind free from dualistic distraction, [success will follow].
This practice of the True Dharma accomplishes mantras and is further able to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings.
If one practices the Dharma in a manner other than this ritual procedure, [the result will be contrary].
If the Dharma is treated as non-Dharma, the mantra will not be accomplished;
such practice is in vain and no merit shall be obtained. The Buddhas of the past have taught this samādhi to benefit all sentient beings.
If those sons of the Buddha are well-versed in this King of Rituals and can properly recite it according to the dharma,
then the characteristics of the mantra will become the path to enlightenment.
Before long, this person shall sit at the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) and fully realize great awakening.
Furthermore, regarding the practitioner who recites the Dharma,
concerning the profound and subtle matters of the mantra rules:
Although one may achieve accomplishment through secret practices,
one must also constantly maintain the categories of precepts, perpetually engage in meditative observation, and continue the recitation of mantras without interruption.
It is like a ritual mandala that, if its construction is incomplete or its offerings deficient, cannot succeed.
One may dwell there for a time;
the ritual methods of the maṇḍala are complete, and one practices with courageous diligence,
reciting and studying in succession without ceasing from samādhi.
The sins accumulated over kalpas shall be eradicated,
and all sentient beings shall obtain merit.
It is like a great wheel-turning monarch who possesses every kind of wealth and treasure in full.
One may enjoy it at will without it ever being exhausted.
This mantra, spoken by the Tathāgata,
is fully endowed with all meritorious qualities.
The Benefit and Happiness of All Sentient Beings is Unending.

Chapter Twelve: The Ritual Rules for the Rosary. At that time, the World-Honored One Śākyamuni...
Observing the assembly of the Śuddhāvāsakāyika devas,
he addressed the youth Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Mañjuśrī, listen attentively now."
This clarifies the practice of mantra recitation for practitioners;
it concerns the recitation of mantras for the sake of all sentient beings,
as well as the methods for the equal accomplishment of various sūtras and dharmas.
"Regarding the ritual rules for the rosary and all mantras,
you should listen attentively and receive them with a profound mind.
When the youth Mañjuśrī heard this, he did so.
He addressed the Blessed One, saying: "Excellent, Blessed One!
We pray that you will explain all those mantra practices, so as to enable all practitioners and all sentient beings [to attain realization]."
Having heard this, they were all enabled to attain samādhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the youth Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Mañjuśrī, listen attentively, listen attentively."
I shall now analyze and explain this in detail for you:
all sentient beings who delight in the practice of mantras,
if they can maintain it with purity, single-minded devotion, and diligent application.
All purposes will be accomplished.
I shall now recite the primary mantra:

Namaḥ samantabuddhānām | ājñāpayatu bhagavān tadyathā | oṃ kuru kuru sarvarthasādha sādhaya sarvaduṣṭavinmukhani gaganamalaśveta viśodhaya svāhā | If there is a practitioner who possesses this mantra...
Whenever one intends to manufacture a rosary,
for the sake of seeking purity in all matters—
from drilling and polishing to stringing and various forms of ritual holding— one must act accordingly.
All undertakings will be fully accomplished.
When first seeing the jewel tree and wishing to gather its fruit,
one must first perform consecration upon that tree and protect oneself.
One must concentrate with a sincere heart and recite this mantra thirty-seven times.
Then, sleep beneath the tree for one night to seek the auspicious or inauspicious signs as responses.
If that person, within a dream,
sees that non-human spirit manifesting a hideous appearance,
the practitioner who maintains the recitation, having recognized it as it truly is, [should act accordingly].
Furthermore, every day at the time of dawn,
he went beneath that tree to look for it;
yet sometimes he could not even find the pearl he intended to gather.
This is a most inauspicious omen.
That practitioner of recitation should quickly distance himself from that tree and go to another place to seek out an auspicious tree.
There are several kinds of jewel trees:
first, the *vajra* fruit; second, the *indrā* fruit.
Third, bodhi seeds;
fourth, huán seeds;
and those possessing the seeds of other trees and so forth.
Once these various fruit-bearing trees have been found,
one should first have a companion climb the tree;
if there is no companion, one should climb the tree oneself and select the highest branch that is fully laden with fruit.
Recite the preceding mantra to empower it.
Whenever that person climbs the tree, their mind shall not become confused or deluded,
up until they reach the top of the tree and its highest branches.
Until one has recovered that son,
this is the supreme jewel;
I declare this jewel to be of the highest utility.
One attains the accomplishment of the supreme dharma.
If one reaches a middle branch, one obtains a middling jewel and attains the accomplishment of the middling dharma.
If one reaches the lower branches and obtains the lower beads,
one shall achieve the most inferior karmic retribution;
as for its seeds, they are thin and shriveled.
Furthermore, those that are worm-eaten are all unfit for use.
If one obtains a bead from a western branch,
by attaining the accomplishment of the rite, one shall obtain wealth.
If one obtains a bead made from the northern branch,
one will be held in high esteem by noble sages, and all yakṣas and bhūtas will be completely subdued.
Even devas, up to gandharvas, kiṃnaras, rākṣasas, and so forth, will all be completely subdued.
If one performs various activities according to the ritual procedures,
all correct undertakings will be augmented;
furthermore, one will attain all accomplishments and obtain whatever is sought.
If one obtains an eastern branch and sees that fruit is still present upon that branch,
and if one takes that seed to serve as a bead,
then any practitioner who performs the cultivation and recitation will attain the accomplishment of a Vidyādhara.
One will achieve perfection in all various undertakings;
by single-mindedly receiving and upholding [this practice], one shall also attain longevity.
If the southern branch is long and leafless, [the result is as follows].
Although that creature has offspring, they cannot serve as beads;
were they to be used as beads, they would harm the lives of sentient beings.
Therefore, those who maintain their recitations should remain single-mindedly detached from them.
If the southern branch is not long or lacks leaves,
or if it has fruits that are fit to be used as beads,
the practitioner who maintains the recitation must likewise abandon it.
Why is this? Because it is still capable of killing one's enemies.
If one relinquishes it and does not grasp it, one will obtain immeasurable merit.
If one obtains a lower branch that grows downward and points toward the earth, even penetrating into the ground...
If there is a fruit on that branch that has become a jewel,
the practitioner who maintains the recitation should, according to the ritual manual, focus their mind and uphold it with devotion.
As for the practitioner of mantra recitation, whether in the mountains or in the valleys, wherever they may be—
In all the empty caves where asuras dwell,
those who maintain their recitations are able to enter them all;
they may even reside together with male and female asuras within the asura palaces.
One shall experience supreme happiness for the duration of one kalpa.
When first obtaining the seed-pearls from the tree and descending from it,
that practitioner of recitation shall chant the aforementioned mantra to perform protection.
One should seek out a pure location and construct it in successive stages,
whether for oneself or for others, according to one's own wishes,
in a place that is distant or near, and where one finds joy in dwelling or intends to reside permanently.
When intending to manufacture [the beads],
one should first purify body and mind individually and maintain focused concentration. Then,
take up the seed-pearls and drill them, holding them steadily while polishing and refining them.
Recite the mantra for each individual item three times,
five times, or twenty-one times.
Once the mantras have been recited, the wise one says:
Now, for the sake of such-and-such a matter, I shall describe each point in detail.
Once the incantations and prayers are completed, the essence of the pearl will attain purity;
thereafter, have a young girl join the threads together.
Then, using threads of five colors, combine them into a single color like a flower garland;
whether combining three or five,
they must be joined tightly according to the requirements of the beads.
The wise person selecting *bodhi* seeds must ensure they are all uniform and of good quality; they must not be decayed or deficient.
They must be complete and, moreover, fine ones are best.
These include *bodhi* seeds, *vajra* seeds, *indrākṣa* seeds, and *śrīphala* seeds.
Furthermore, one should select individual, exceptionally fine, and superior materials;
the practitioner performing the recitation must accomplish this with single-minded concentration.
Alternatively, one may use gold, silver, pearls, crystal, tridacna shell, or agate.
As well as corals and various other jewels,
or using the most supreme maṇi gems and so forth,
they must be perfectly complete and lustrous, without any deficiency or reduction.
Whenever threading [the beads], one must focus the mind with concentration and not allow it to become distracted.
Once the rosary is completed, all petitions and aspirations will swiftly receive a miraculous response.
If the aforementioned materials—such as seeds from various trees or precious gems—are unavailable:
It is also permissible to tie it using only *kuśa* grass.
The number of beads is not fixed, as there are three grades:
the superior grade consists of one hundred and eight.
There are fifty-four of the middle grade and twenty-seven of the lower grade;
there is also a separate most superior grade, for which one thousand and eighty should be used as the count.
Furthermore, there are those cast from gold, silver, copper, iron, brass, lead, tin, and so forth;
or made by casting one, two, or three of these metals together.
One should seek only that they be solid and complete, ensuring they are free from any defects or deficiencies.
It must nevertheless be luminous, brilliant, and pure, like a precious necklace.
Any practitioner who maintains the recitation of mantras must maintain the purity of their precepts;
furthermore, they should proceed to a river of flowing water.
Having finished bathing with separate pure water for cleansing,
one should first rub the rosary with clean earth and then wash it with water;
thereafter, one should further wash it with the five fragrant waters.
Furthermore, having finished rubbing and wiping [the beads] with excellent ointments, superior white sandalwood incense,
and perfumed waters such as *kunkuma*,
the practitioner who maintains the recitation shall take these beads and proceed to a place where a Buddha image is located.
Whether the image of the Buddha is sculpted or painted,
one should seek the most excellently adorned and supreme image of Śākyamuni Buddha, the Teacher of Gods and Humans.
In accordance with the Buddha’s words, one should demarcate the boundary of the site and install the Buddha image therein.
In front of that Buddha, sit with the body erect and upright,
focusing the mind single-pointedly, and recite the mantra one thousand and eighty times,
or one hundred and eight times.
He cupped it in both hands and offered it to his original teacher, Śākyamuni Buddha.
Having made the offering to the Buddha,
he placed this jewel directly before him.
When this jewel is released, it appears like the form of a circular mandala,
or like the coiled form of a serpent entwined;
that practitioner who maintains the recitation reaches the night.
He simply spread grass upon the ground before the Buddha and slept there to seek the aforementioned signs;
if, within his dreams, he should see the Buddha, pratyekabuddhas, śrāvakas, or other such signs.
Whatever that person seeks will certainly be accomplished.
If one sees a youth,
or sees various appearances of a young boy, [the goal will be achieved].
Furthermore, one obtains a rosary to offer in worship;
by reciting the dhāraṇī, that practitioner attains all accomplishments,
or perceives other auspicious signs, whereby everything sought becomes easily obtained.
Chapter Thirteen: The Chapter on Homa. From the *Mañjuśrī-mūla-kalpa*, the Extensive Vaipulya Scripture of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka. At that time, the World-Honored One, Śākyamuni Buddha, [spoke].
Furthermore, having observed the assembly of the Śuddhāvāsakāyika devas,
he addressed the youth Mañjuśrī, saying: "Mañjuśrī,
you should now extensively explain the supreme ritual procedures for the recitation of sublime mantras, homa, and other such matters."
If there are those who, by relying on practice, attain the accomplishment of a Vidyādhara,
I shall now explain the supreme ritual procedures for all the subtle practices of the Fire Deity (Agnideva) during the retreat.
What are those matters, such as the practice of the Vidyādhara, for all those practitioners?
I shall now first proclaim the secret heart-mantra of the Fire Deity (*Agni*).
It is: *Oṃ uttiṣṭha hṛdbiṅgāra lohita kṣaṇi he naya paca hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ sarvavijñānān śamaya svāhā*. Mañjuśrī, this is the supreme heart-vidyā of the Fire Deity.
If one wishes to achieve all accomplishments in whatever actions one undertakes,
one must always first maintain the recitation of this heart-mantra of the Great Fire Deity (Mahātejas).
One should perform the rite of homa by consecrating clarified butter (*ghṛta*) three times.
I pray that the Fire Deity (Agni) will surely descend.
If there is a practitioner who performs the three types of rites according to the ritual rules—
namely, the rites of pacification (śāntika), enrichment (pauṣṭika), and subjugation (abhicārika)— [the deity shall grant success].
Regarding the method for using dry or moist firewood—whether long or short, thick or thin—as well as whether it is suitable for use:
generally, for rites of pacification (*śāntika*), one should use firewood from the *aśoka* tree.
This wood should be one or two feet in length and three finger-widths in thickness, and it must be moist and lustrous.
If used according to the ritual, one will certainly obtain auspiciousness.
However, if it is withered, decayed, half-burnt,
or infested by insects, it is unfit for use.
Alternatively, for those who use leaves, they must be green or white;
if they are black, partially burnt, or contain insect holes and the like,
they are also unfit for use.
The homa hearth must not be made too high.
In selecting a site for the hearth, one must choose an excellent and pure location,
such as a mountain range, a riverbank, or a place of retreat.
One may practice in a cold forest or an empty house;
one may also do so on a mountain peak, in an empty monastery, or in a vast wilderness.
These are the supreme places for spiritual cultivation taught by all the Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
Once the site has been selected,
one must first excavate the ground to a depth of one cubit, or three or four cubits,
and remove all inauspicious objects from within it.
If it is a place naturally pure throughout its extent, free from all impurities,
one need only dig down to a depth of one cubit and seek out excellent earth to fill it within.
The hearth is only two cubits wide;
it may be circular, square, or crescent-shaped,
with its perimeter plastered and decorated with a lotus border.
In the center, place a three-pronged vajra.
Having placed the vajra,
prepare all the materials required for the homa.
Furthermore, one should prepare a seat of grass mats and place it one cubit away from the altar.
The practitioner performing the recitation should sit upon these mats and carry out the homa rites.
If that person seeks the most supreme goal, it will be swiftly accomplished.
First, one must resolve within one's own mind and not give rise to doubt or hesitation.
If performing the rite for pacification (*śāntika*), one should sit facing east;
if performing the rite for enrichment (*pauṣṭika*), one should sit facing north.
If performing a rite of subjugation, one should sit facing south.
If that practitioner of recitation wishes for the accomplishment of their task,
they must constantly maintain the recitation without interruption.
When performing the homa,
one should use fuel sticks of bilva wood,
arka wood, plakṣa wood, and nyagrodha wood.
All the aforementioned woods must be moistened for use in rites of pacification (*śānti*) and enrichment (*puṣṭi*).
If they are to be used for subjugation (*abhicāra*), they should be dry and withered.
If the wood is from the *āmra* tree, or if it has a single-pointed tip,
none of these may be used for rites of enrichment (*puṣṭi*), pacification (*śānti*), or similar purposes.
If there is no damp firewood, use dry wood instead.
When using it, wrap it completely with soft, tender, green *kuśa* grass,
which is lush and supple like the neck of a peacock.
Such rules shall be established as the constant standard.
If the grass is red or withered and dry, it must not be used.
If one uses it, I declare that this person incurs immeasurable transgression.
When performing the homa, one should seek water that is constantly pure and free of insects for the purpose of sprinkling purification (prokṣaṇa).
Having sprinkled it thoroughly three times all around, one should place it in the location of the Fire Deity (Agnideva).
Furthermore, take a handful of grass or more and bind it into a bundle;
place it near your hand where you intend to light it.
While it has not yet caught fire, do not blow on it with your mouth.
One should use cloth, leaves, or the hands and so forth to fan the fire;
one must use a fan or clean cloth to kindle it.
Once the fire has been lit, the practitioner should maintain the recitation.
When performing the homa and other rites for three repetitions, one attains purification by sprinkling.
With the right hand, perform the homa by taking three morsels of food and tossing them;
having offered these along with ghee, milk, and other foods, cast them as oblations.
Recite the root mantra.
Pay homage to the Original Teacher Śākyamuni Buddha and to all Buddhas, prostrating as you wish.
Next, recite the heart-mantra of the Fire Deity seven times to invite that deity,
and further offer excellent incense and flowers as an invitation.
Then, the practitioner and the wise person shall sit in their respective seats.
Do not employ any other mantras.
First, mix rice grains, honey, and curdled milk together;
then, using three pieces of moistened wood, perform the homa for the Fire Deity.
If for the purpose of rites of increase or mantra practices,
one should dip both ends [of the thread];
then, when about to perform the ritual, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times (one lakṣa).
Recite either one thousand and eight or one hundred and eight times from the very beginning;
for each recitation, cast a piece of firewood into the fire.
One must continue until the count is complete without interruption.
The firewood, as well as the curd, milk, honey, and so forth required for the rite, must be prepared in advance;
they must not be lacking when the time comes to perform the ritual.
One who performs homa must first understand the characteristics of the fire’s smoke and flames,
as well as the methods for auspicious accomplishment or non-accomplishment.
If one performs a homa for the pacification of calamities (śāntika),...
When the flames blaze intensely as a single mass and are further accompanied by the absence of smoke, this is an auspicious sign;
the same applies to rites of increase (*puṣṭi*).
The presence of smoke is an inauspicious sign for rites of subjugation (*abhicāra*);
it is not protected by the Buddha.
If it is for a rite of pacification (*śāntika*), one should obtain white flames.
This is the mark of supreme auspiciousness.
Through its practice, one attains the accomplishment of mantras;
if it is red in color, one attains the accomplishment of increase.
If the smoke appears dark red or black,
one will likewise attain three kinds of accomplishment;
if it takes on the color of clouds or various other forms, [the same applies].
The activities he performs and his mantras will all fail to achieve accomplishment.
When the flames blaze intensely,
one may therein perceive the color of the great earth and various other signs.
Furthermore, beginning again as at the initial commencement according to the ritual rules,
one should once more perform the recitation, homa, and so forth.
When auspicious signs appear, one shall attain the accomplishment of the mantra.
All the mantras for the previously explained maṇḍala rituals, the performance of homa,
and the rites of inviting and dismissing the fire deity and others,
were personally proclaimed by the Buddhas and Tathāgatas of the past.
If there is a practitioner who, before that image of the Buddha,
with a fierce and sharp mind and without giving rise to doubt,

And this mantra can bestow happiness.

If one performs extensive virtuous deeds according to the Dharma and constantly recites [the mantra] one thousand and eight times,

In the final age after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa,
by reciting according to the Dharma, one will swiftly attain accomplishment.

up to the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Ratnaketu.

As for those noble assemblies,

In the world of Amitāyus,

In the final age of the Dharma, when the teaching is about to perish,

That Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra transmitted it to the Youth Mañjuśrī. Youth,
I now likewise give rise to profound compassion for all sentient beings.

Listen attentively, young man.
I shall now further explain the ritual procedure for the great power of your mantra,
should you wish to accomplish all activities.
First, in a pure place upon a mountain,

Taking milk as one’s food, one should silently recite [the mantra].
One must not give rise to thoughts regarding other mantra methods;
rather, one should resolve upon bodhicitta, take refuge in the Triple Gem, and maintain pure precepts.

Having thus cultivated purity,
one may then perform the rites for the various supreme accomplishments (*siddhi*).
One who wishes to perform this rite should first seek out an artist whose mind is fundamentally pure and who has received the precepts;
one should also seek the finest, most excellent pigments.
Having obtained these, one may then prepare the cloth painting (*paṭa*).
The cloth should be one cubit in width and four feet in length.
Having prepared it in this manner, [one proceeds].
Having sprinkled it clean with perfumed water made from sandalwood, camphor, saffron,
and so forth, the painter shall be purified;
he shall eat the three white foods and wear fresh, clean garments.
On an auspicious day during the waxing moon, or on the fifteenth day,
begin drawing at sunrise and continue until noon;

In this manner, he continued day after day until the painting was completed.
On the scroll, he first depicted the world of Amitāyus,
with its ground entirely covered with various precious lotus flowers.
It is adorned above and below with great blue jewels, crystal jewels, and large green jewels; in its center,
one should paint a great jeweled palace.
The banners, streamers, parasols, and all manner of offering implements were all exceptionally exquisite and further possessed blazing flames;
each covered the space above in magnificent splendor.
In the center of the first hall, a lion throne is depicted.
Upon the throne, the Tathāgata Amitāyus-jñāna-niścaya-rāja is painted in the posture of preaching the Dharma.
The Buddha’s body is crimson in color, with radiance shining in the four directions.
On the left, paint a seat of precious *utpala* lotuses.

his right hand holds a white fly-whisk, and his left hand grasps a celestial fruit.
It is made with a light of pale green radiating everywhere,
adorned and embellished with various ornaments.
To the right, one should paint the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Samantabhadra.
He sits upon a precious utpala lotus throne, his body is light green in color.
He wears a jeweled crown and exquisite blue robes;
pearl necklaces and jeweled garlands drape across his shoulders.
The blazing light universally adorns all things.
To the right, next, one should paint the noble Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī,
seated upon a precious utpala flower throne, his body golden-yellow in color.
He has the appearance of a youth with five topknots on his head;
his face is upright and majestic, endowed with all the primary marks.
He wears a wondrous blue garment and is adorned with genuine jewels.
Wearing necklaces and shoulder-ornaments to adorn his body,
he stands with palms joined in joy, gazing up at the Tathāgata.
Next, below him, one should paint the practitioner reciting the mantra.
Adorned with her own natural grace and radiant purity,
she touches the ground with her right knee and holds a lotus garland in her hand,
bowing her head in a gesture of offering.
Next, on the right side of the upper corner of the cloth painting, depict two Buddhas:
the first named Amitābha (Immeasurable Light) and the second named Puṇyaprabha (Merit Light).
On the left side, depict two Buddhas.
The first was named Sālavatīrāja and the second Ratnaketu.
The bodies of these four Tathāgatas were like gold, radiating brilliant light;
they sat upon white lotus thrones adorned with various flowers.
Adorned with various ornaments, most subtle and supreme,
he sits in the full lotus posture (paryaṅka) in the gesture of preaching the Dharma.
Above all the Buddhas, one should paint various clouds.
Within the clouds, one should depict a bodhisattva named Wondrous Eye (Sudṛśa).
His physical marks are fully perfected and his radiance shines everywhere.
His right hand performs the gesture of granting boons (varada-mudrā), and his left hand holds the corner of a monastic robe (kāṣāya).
In accordance with that mode of practice, one should rain down various flowers from within the clouds as an offering to the Tathāgata.
This is the ritual procedure for the painted scroll (*paṭavidhāna*) of the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, King of Certainty in Immeasurable Life Wisdom.
It possesses the power of that single-syllable mantra,
as well as the inconceivable, vast merit and supreme power of the Sovereign Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa King, the Great Wheel Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa King, Vīrya, and others.
I have briefly explained this.

If there is a practitioner who wishes to perform the rites of accomplishment,

By virtue of the majestic power of the heart-mind of the Tathāgata King of Certainty of Immeasurable Life Wisdom, and of all Tathāgatas,

This is the Single-Syllable Great Wheel-King of the Heart of the Youth Mañjuśrī.

Visualize that all one's requests are fulfilled by the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
